Where peat burns, and how close together

  • Show All Code

TAKE-HOME EXERCISE 1

A first- and second-order point-pattern analysis of VIIRS active-fire detections in Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, 1 July to 25 September 2026.

Author
Affiliation

Jedidiah Asaf Tallulembang

ISSS626 Geospatial Analytics and Applications

Published

September 26, 2026

Abstract

I analyse VIIRS active-fire detections over Pulang Pisau Regency, Central Kalimantan, for the 2026 dry season. I picked this regency because it has the highest detection density of any Kalimantan regency big enough for second-order estimation at the kilometre scale. I wanted to answer three things: where the detections concentrate, whether they interact beyond that concentration, and what a fire agency could honestly do with the answer.

The thing that shaped the whole analysis is a distinction I nearly missed. A VIIRS hotspot is a 375 m pixel seen during one satellite overpass, not a fire. I measured the consequence: the raw detection count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. So testing the raw pattern against complete spatial randomness rejects the null overwhelmingly and tells me nothing, because the sensor guarantees that result. I switched the unit of analysis to the 375 m cell and the null to an inhomogeneous Poisson process, re-estimating the reference intensity for every simulated pattern. That gives a test that could fail. It does not.

What I found: clustering beyond the trend is strongest at about 440 m and only decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7 km. That last number corrects my own first attempt, which capped the distance range at 5 km and concluded the excess stopped at 2 km. A Thomas process fitted after removing the trend puts the dominant cluster scale at 1.1 km, with 95% of a cluster inside 2.6 km. Fitted without removing the trend it returns 3.3 km and 440 events per cluster, which is really just the peat belt re-described as a few giant clusters. A Knox permutation test finds space-time interaction concentrated within a few hundred metres and a few days. Distance to the road network accounts for 1,991 of the 2,005 AIC units separating my covariate model from an intercept-only model, while mapped drainage accounts for almost none, which turned out to say more about OpenStreetMap coverage than about drainage.

R sf spatstat NASA FIRMS KDE Kinhom Knox test Thomas process

Executive summary, 10 slides · Repository

1 Introduction and study context

Indonesian Borneo burns every dry season, and when I started reading about it I learned that the fires which matter most for public health are not forest fires in the ordinary sense. They are peat fires. Drained tropical peat is a metres-deep carbon store that, once dry, smoulders below the surface for weeks. You cannot put it out by suppressing a surface flame front, and it releases a dense particulate smoke that carries hundreds of kilometres. So the public-safety burden is respiratory rather than thermal: school closures, airport closures, and a measurable excess of acute respiratory cases across Central Kalimantan and, in bad years, across the Malacca Strait.

Pulang Pisau Regency sits at the centre of this. Its southern half was the site of the Mega Rice Project, a 1990s programme that cut thousands of kilometres of drainage canal into deep peat and was then abandoned. The canals are still there, the water table is still lowered, and the land is still unusually combustible. That is why I did not treat the regency as just a convenient study window. It is a place where the link between land management and public-safety outcomes is about as visible as it gets.

Fire detections are point events in space and time, so point-pattern analysis is the obvious tool. What I wanted to work out in this exercise is what that tool can honestly support once you take the data seriously.

1.1 The problem the data handed me

I need to state one thing before any analysis, because it ended up governing every interpretation I made.

A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel in which a radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during a single overpass. A large peat fire covering ten square kilometres produces many dozens of detections in one pass, and the two satellites pass overhead roughly four times a day between them, so the same fire gets detected over and over. What a detection actually records is the sensor sampling fire, not fire occurrence. Any statistic I compute on the raw detection set is therefore partly measuring the instrument.

Once I realised that, the textbook second-order question stopped being interesting. “Is this pattern clustered relative to complete spatial randomness” already has a known answer before I compute anything. It is clustered, overwhelmingly, and it would still be clustered even if fires were sited completely at random, because each fire produces a burst of adjacent detections. Reporting that rejection as a finding would be close to meaningless, so I did not want to build the report on it.

Instead I changed two things, and I am stating them up front because they are the real methodological content of this exercise rather than housekeeping. I changed the unit of analysis from the detection to the 375 m cell, and I changed the null model from complete spatial randomness to an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Section 7 is where that pays off.

2 Research questions and objectives

I set four questions, each with a null and a reason for asking it. I wrote these before running the second-order analysis, so the report can be read as a test of them rather than as a description of whatever came out.

Q1. How does the intensity of fire detection vary across the regency, and at what spatial scale is that variation stable? First-order. I ask it because a fire agency allocates fixed resources to places, so what is useful to them is a surface, not a test. I added the scale qualifier because a kernel estimate can be made to show almost any structure depending on the bandwidth, so I do not think the question is answerable unless I also defend that choice.

Q2. How does intensity vary in time, and is the temporal signal a property of fire activity or of the observing system? First-order. I split this out because the two satellites observe at fixed local times, so any apparent daily cycle is a sampling artefact. I wanted to be sure I did not read the orbit as fire behaviour.

Q3. Once large-scale variation in intensity is accounted for, is there residual interaction between events, and over what distance? Second-order. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) estimated by kernel smoothing. Rejecting this null tells me something that rejecting complete spatial randomness does not, because the inhomogeneous null already contains everything my first-order analysis found. The “over what distance” part is the bit with operational value, and it is also the part I initially got wrong.

Q4. Is there space-time interaction, over and above the separate spatial and temporal patterns? Second-order, spatio-temporal. My null is random labelling: I hold the observed locations and the observed set of dates fixed and permute only the pairing between them. This conditions on both marginal patterns, which matters, because it means a rejection cannot be explained away by the seasonal ramp or by the spatial concentration. I already know both of those exist.

I added a fifth question as a value-added extension in Section 9, because the four above tell me clustering exists without telling me what it is organised around or how big a cluster actually is.

3 Data and study design

3.1 Sources

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Item, ~Detail,
  "Event data", "NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, near-real-time (NRT)",
  "Platforms", "Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, both retained",
  "Access route", "FIRMS `area` REST API, CSV, 5-day request blocks",
  "Access date", format(ACCESS_DATE, "%d %B %Y"),
  "Spatial extent requested", "108.5 to 119.1 E, 5.2 S to 4.5 N (all Kalimantan)",
  "Boundaries", "geoBoundaries gbOpen Indonesia ADM1 and ADM2, commit 9469f09",
  "Boundary vintage", "2020, sourced from BPS Statistics Indonesia via OCHA",
  "Boundary licence", "CC BY 3.0 IGO",
  "Covariates", "OpenStreetMap via Overpass: `highway`, `waterway`",
  "Software", glue("R {getRversion()}, sf {packageVersion('sf')}, spatstat.explore {packageVersion('spatstat.explore')}")
) |> kable()

3.2 Why I chose this regency

I chose the study window with a rule applied to the whole island, after downloading data for all 56 Kalimantan regencies and cities and screening it for confidence. The rule: the highest detection density among regencies large enough to support second-order estimation to a 5 km lag, which I operationalised as an area above 5,000 km².

I used density rather than raw count because intensity relative to window area is what governs how much signal a point pattern carries. I added the size floor because a 5 km lag inside a small window starts to approach the window’s own dimension, and at that point edge effects dominate every second-order estimate I would compute.

code 
RANK |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    Regency = shapeName, Province = province,
    Detections = fmt_n(n_detections),
    `Area (km²)` = fmt_n(round(area_km2)),
    `Per 1,000 km²` = fmt_n(round(per_1000km2))
  ) |> kable(align = "llrrr")

Pulang Pisau wins on that rule outright, at 3656 detections per 1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.

Ketapang beat it on absolute count, with 65,901 detections against Pulang Pisau’s 35,679. I did not choose it because it covers 29,722 km², slightly over three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its bigger count is mostly just a bigger window.

Kota Palangka Raya has the highest density of any unit at 8,222 per 1,000 km², but covers only 2,606 km². A 5 km lag there is a large fraction of the window’s own width, so edge effects would drive my second-order results rather than the fires.

Pulang Pisau also comes rank 2 of 56 on raw count, so I am not selecting some obscure unit to make the rule work. Its window of 9,759 km², at 86 km by 213 km, comfortably supports estimation to a 5 km lag.

I should be open about how I got here. My first pass selected the regency from a seven-day sample of the same feed, on which Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full 87-day window it does not, Ketapang does. So I restated the selection rule against the complete record and re-applied it. I am reporting that rather than quietly fixing it, because a rule chosen after you have seen which unit it favours is not really a rule, and I would rather the reader be able to judge that for themselves.

3.3 Point event definition

I define an event as one 375 m grid cell in which at least one qualifying VIIRS detection was recorded. Qualifying means all of the following, and I have given the reason for each rather than just the rule.

Sensor and product
VIIRS 375 m I-band, Collection 2, S-NPP or NOAA-20. MODIS is excluded: its 1 km footprint is coarser than the distances this analysis is about, so including it would blur the very scale under study.
Confidence
Nominal or high. Low-confidence detections are dropped. They are dominated by small or cool anomalies and by edge-of-scan geometry, so retaining them would make apparent intensity vary with viewing angle rather than with fire.
Coordinates
Present, finite, within valid latitude and longitude ranges, and not the (0, 0) sentinel that some pipelines emit for a failed geolocation.
Timestamp
A parseable UTC acquisition time. Converted to WITA (UTC+8), because the definition of a fire day and any reading of diurnal behaviour must be local.
Location
Strictly within the Pulang Pisau polygon. This also serves as the offshore screen, since the polygon is terrestrial.
Not a fixed installation
See the persistence screen below. This substitutes for a field the NRT product does not carry.
Deduplicated
Exact duplicate records removed, then collapsed to one event per 375 m cell per local day.

I build three patterns from the same screened detections, because which unit is right depends on which question I am asking:

Pattern Unit Used for
ppp_all every retained detection sensitivity checks only
ppp_daycell one event per 375 m cell per local day spatio-temporal analysis
ppp_cell one event per 375 m cell over the window primary spatial analysis

I use ppp_cell as the primary spatial pattern because it removes the repeat-detection inflation I described in Section 1.1. A cell that burned for three weeks and was detected eighty times contributes one point, not eighty.

For the representative point of each cell I take the earliest detection in it. That is deterministic and it keeps a real sensor coordinate. I considered snapping to cell centres and rejected it, because that would impose a regular lattice and manufacture apparent regularity at small lags, which would contaminate exactly the statistic the rest of the report depends on.

3.4 Spatial study window

My window is the Pulang Pisau administrative polygon, unbuffered, in WGS 84 / UTM zone 49S (EPSG:32749).

Projecting is not optional here. Every second-order statistic I use is a function of Euclidean distance in metres, and at this latitude one degree of longitude is about 111 km while one degree of latitude is about 110.6 km. If I worked in degrees I would be building a systematic anisotropy into every distance I compute. Zone 49S is the right one for a regency centroid at 113.96°E, which sits inside the zone’s 108°E to 114°E span. I checked the eastern edge, which reaches 114.35°E and is marginally outside, and the resulting scale error is below 0.1%, so it does not matter at the kilometre scales I work at.

I used the administrative boundary rather than a buffered or natural window because the management question is administrative: a regency fire agency has jurisdiction to that line. The cost is a real edge effect, since fires obviously do not stop at a boundary, and I handle it with edge correction rather than pretending it is not there (Section 5).

3.5 Temporal study window

1 July to 25 September 2026, 87 days. The lower bound was imposed on me rather than chosen, and I want to state the constraint precisely, because it is the kind of thing that is easy to misrepresent by accident.

code 
PROBE$nrt |> transmute(Date = format(date, "%d %b %Y"),
                       `Detections returned` = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "lr")

The FIRMS area endpoint serves near-real-time granules on a rolling retention of roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing archive that would have covered January to June has not been produced for 2026. So the earliest day I can retrieve is 1 July 2026, which I located to the day with the probe above rather than assuming it. The upper bound is my choice: the last complete UTC day before I accessed the data, so that no partially observed day enters the daily series and shows up as a fake decline.

I want to be careful not to oversell the window. It is what was available. But it does happen to span the onset, escalation and peak of the 2026 dry season, which is the period a fire agency actually acts over. If the retention limit had cut off the peak instead of the wet-season baseline I would have had to change the study design entirely. The honest cost is that I cannot make any wet-season comparison, so nothing in this report speaks to the seasonal amplitude of fire activity, only to its structure within one season. I repeat that in Section 12 because it is a real limit on what I can claim.

3.6 My completeness audit, and a real outage

Counting the rows I downloaded does not tell me the record is complete. The failure mode I was worried about is a request that comes back empty, because that is indistinguishable from a day on which nothing burned, and it would show up in my analysis as a drop in fire activity that never happened.

So I built the audit to catch exactly that. Each of the two platforms should contribute at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan on every day of an 87-day dry season, because an island-sized box is never completely without fire. Any day where a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure and worth chasing.

code 
GAP$missing_after |> transmute(Date = format(dt, "%d %B %Y"),
                               `Platform absent` = platform) |> kable(align = "ll")

Six of the seven dates are consecutive, which made me suspect a real outage rather than a flaky connection. Re-querying confirmed it: Suomi NPP returns an empty result for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August no matter how many times I ask. So this is an absence in the FIRMS near-real-time record itself, not a transient request failure I could fix by retrying. On those seven days my analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone, and detection counts are depressed by roughly the contribution of one platform.

The consequence is small, but I do not want to write it off as nothing. Those dates carry 51 of 23,576 events, or 0.22% of the record, and all of them fall in the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the affected dates are 7.3 against 10.8 on nearby unaffected July dates, which is consistent with losing one platform on very small counts. No conclusion I draw turns on those seven days, but the reader should treat the early-season part of my daily series as a slight underestimate.

4 Data preparation and quality assessment

4.1 The audit trail

I counted every exclusion. The table below is generated by the pipeline rather than typed in by me, so it cannot drift away from what the code actually did.

code 
P$qa |> transmute(Step = step, Rule = rule,
                  `In` = fmt_n(n_in), Removed = fmt_n(n_removed), `Out` = fmt_n(n_out)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrr")

Three things I want to point out about this table.

The biggest single reduction is the spatial clip, and that is expected. I downloaded all of Kalimantan so that I could justify my choice of regency against the alternatives, and the overwhelming majority of those detections are outside Pulang Pisau.

The coordinate and timestamp screens removed nothing at all. I am flagging that rather than skipping past it, because in my experience a cleaning step that catches nothing is often a cleaning step that is not actually testing what it says it is. I checked mine against deliberately broken records while developing the pipeline, and they do fire. The FIRMS product is simply well-formed here: every record had finite coordinates in range and a parseable timestamp. I kept the screens in because I want the pipeline to be re-runnable against other windows and products where that will not be true.

The confidence screen removed 4.1% of records, and exact duplicate removal a further 0 rows, confirming that the API does deliver a small number of repeated granule records.

code 
P$conf_tab |> transmute(Confidence = confidence, Detections = fmt_n(n),
                        Share = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")

4.2 The missing type field, and what I replaced it with

This was the data-quality problem that took me longest to solve. The FIRMS standard-processing product carries a type field separating vegetation fire (0) from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT product I have to use does not carry it, which I verified against the API response header rather than assuming: column present = FALSE. So I had to reconstruct the screen it would have given me.

I worked through the three cases separately:

  • Volcanoes (type 1) are not a risk at all. Borneo has no Holocene volcano, so this screen is unnecessary rather than approximated. I did not need to do anything.
  • Offshore (type 3) is already handled by my clip to the terrestrial polygon.
  • Other static land sources (type 2) are a genuine problem. Kalimantan has palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, and all of them show up as persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case I actually had to solve.

My substitute is a persistence screen. The logic is that a vegetation fire burns out or moves, whereas a flare stack does not. So I score each 375 m cell by the number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day window, and drop cells above a threshold as fixed installations.

code 
P$persist_sens |> transmute(
  `Threshold (share of days)` = percent(threshold, accuracy = 1),
  `Cells removed` = fmt_n(n_cells),
  `Detections removed` = fmt_n(n_detections)) |> kable(align = "lrr")

My screen removed nothing. My first reaction was that I had written it wrong, so I checked it two ways, and I now think the empty result is correct.

First, no cell comes anywhere near the threshold. The most persistent cell in the whole window was detected on 21 of 87 days, which is 24.1%. A flare stack or mill would be detected on most clear-sky overpasses across the entire window, so nothing here behaves like one.

Second, I used radiative power as an independent check, because it separates the two cases without relying on persistence at all. A fixed industrial source emits a high and steady radiative power, while smouldering peat emits a low one.

code 
P$persist_top |> transmute(
  Cell = cell, Detections = n_det, `Days detected` = n_days,
  `Share of window` = percent(day_frac, accuracy = 0.1),
  `Mean FRP (MW)` = mean_frp) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")

The median FRP across all my retained detections is 4.2 MW, and the most persistent cells range from 2.9 to 9.1 MW. They are not brighter than the population at all. They are ordinary peat fires that happened to recur in the same cell.

That fits the regency’s land use. Pulang Pisau is peatland and smallholder agriculture, without the gas processing or open-cut coal operations that generate persistent thermal anomalies elsewhere in Kalimantan. If I had picked a window in East Kalimantan instead, I think this screen would have been doing real work.

I report the sensitivity across thresholds rather than a single number on purpose. If the result swung sharply depending on where I put the line, that would be a decision dressed up as a method, and the reader deserves to see which one it is.

4.3 My evidence that a detection is not a fire

The claim I made in Section 1.1 is checkable, so I checked it. If detections were independent events, most occupied cells would be detected exactly once. They are not.

code 
mt <- P$multiplicity
ggplot(mt, aes(n_det, n_cells)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n_det, yend = 0), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Detections recorded in the cell", y = "Number of cells",
       title = "One fire, many detections",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(sum(mt$n_cells))} occupied cells. Median {median(rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells))} detections per cell, ",
                       "maximum {max(mt$n_det)}.")) +
  theme_ex01()
Warning in scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)):
log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.

Only 34.2% of occupied cells were detected exactly once. The mean is 3.4 detections per occupied cell, so the raw count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about 3.4. That is the number that convinced me. Analysing the raw detections as a point pattern would mean analysing the satellite’s revisit schedule about as much as the fire regime, which is why I made ppp_cell the primary unit.

code 
tibble::tibble(
  Pattern = c("`ppp_all`", "`ppp_daycell`", "`ppp_cell`"),
  Unit = c("retained detection", "cell-day", "cell"),
  n = c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n),
  `Mean intensity (per 1,000 km²)` = round(c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n) / P$area_km2 * 1000)
) |> mutate(n = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "llrr")
Warning in env[[name]] <- x: unable to translate 'Mean intensity (per 1,000
km<U+00B2>)' to native encoding

4.4 Geometry validation

I checked the boundary polygon for validity before using it. It is a single valid polygon, so I did not need any multipart or self-intersection handling, though I ran st_make_valid anyway as a defensive step. For point-in-polygon assignment I used st_within rather than st_intersects, so a detection sitting exactly on the boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency. spatstat’s window conversion reported no points rejected as outside the window, which tells me my clip and the owin agree.

Two things here commonly go wrong and I handled them deliberately. First, I assigned regencies to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching. Nearest feature would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell marginally outside its own province, and I would never have noticed. Second, I read the 159 MB national ADM2 file through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather than loading it and subsetting afterwards, so the full national geometry is never held in memory.

5 Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions

Listing assumptions is easy. What I found harder, and more useful, was working out where each one might actually fail, so I have written each with the reason I think it could break rather than just the statement.

A1. Detections are a censored observation of fire, not a sample of fires
VIIRS detects fires above a size and temperature threshold that varies with scan angle, cloud and canopy. Smouldering sub-surface peat combustion, the dominant mode in this landscape, is systematically under-detected because its surface signature is weak. So what I am analysing is the pattern of detectable fire. That biases against exactly the fire type I care most about for public health, and I have no correction available within this data source. My intensity estimates are therefore a lower bound, and their spatial variation is partly variation in detectability rather than in fire.
A2. Cloud cover is not spatially confounded with fire location
I assume this and I cannot fully defend it. Dry-season convection over Borneo is not spatially uniform, and smoke itself attenuates the signal. If cloud were systematically thicker over one part of the regency, apparent intensity there would be depressed and I would read it as less fire. I cannot establish the direction of that bias from the detection data alone.
A3. The window is fixed and known, and events outside it are irrelevant
This is false as physics and I adopt it as a management framing. Fires cross the regency boundary constantly. That is why I edge-correct every second-order estimate, and why I report how sensitive my conclusions are to the correction rather than assuming it away.
A4. The 375 m cell is the finest meaningful spatial resolution
This follows from the sensor rather than from any choice of mine. It imposes a hard minimum separation between distinct events, and I can see it in the pair correlation function as apparent inhibition below roughly 400 m. That inhibition is a property of the instrument. Reading it as fires avoiding one another would be a serious mistake, and an easy one to make.
A5. For the spatial analysis, time is collapsed
My `ppp_cell` pattern treats a cell burning in July and a cell burning in September as the same kind of point. That is fine for "where does fire occur over a season" and wrong for "where is fire now". I relax it in Section 8.
A6. The intensity used as the inhomogeneous null is estimable from the data
This is the weakest link in my second-order analysis and I want to be upfront about it. Estimating $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ from the same pattern I am testing lets the estimate absorb some of the clustering under test, which pushes the envelope outward and makes my test conservative. I mitigate it two ways: I pick a bandwidth that describes broad trend rather than local structure, and I re-estimate $\hat{\lambda}$ for every simulated pattern so the data and the simulations get identical treatment. The bias that remains pushes me toward failing to detect clustering, which is why I am reasonably confident the clustering I do detect is not an artefact of this choice.
A7. Isotropy
$K$, $L$ and $g$ all assume it, because they average over direction. I doubt it holds here: peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines, so I would expect real anisotropy. Any directional structure gets averaged into a weaker isotropic signal, so once again my reported clustering is a conservative reading rather than an inflated one.
A8. Random labelling is the right null for space-time interaction
Permuting time labels across fixed locations conditions on both marginals. That makes it the correct null for "is there interaction beyond the two separate patterns" and the wrong null for "is the seasonal ramp real", which it simply assumes. I intend that. I establish the ramp in Section 6 and I am not trying to test it here.

5.1 My decisions, and what I rejected

code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Decision, ~Choice, ~`Rejected alternative and why`,
  "Coordinate system", "EPSG:32749, UTM 49S", "Geographic coordinates: distance-based statistics require equal units",
  "Event unit", "one 375 m cell", "raw detections: inflates n by ~4x and measures revisit schedule",
  "Representative point", "earliest detection in cell", "cell centre: imposes a lattice, manufactures small-scale regularity",
  "Sensor", "VIIRS 375 m only", "adding MODIS 1 km: coarser than the scales under study",
  "Bandwidth", "fixed 4 km, justified against the interaction range", "bw.ppl and bw.diggle at ~0.6 km: absorb the clustering the second-order test is meant to detect",
  "Kernel", "Gaussian, isotropic", "quartic: negligible difference, less standard diagnostics",
  "Edge correction, KDE", "Diggle's correction", "none: 86 km-wide window, boundary understated",
  "Edge correction, K and L", "border", "Ripley isotropic: cost not justified at this n",
  "r range, K and L", "0 to 5 km", "larger: elongated window makes long lags unreliable",
  "Null model, primary", "inhomogeneous Poisson", "CSR: rejected trivially, uninformative",
  "Envelope construction", "lambda re-estimated per simulation", "fixed lambda: absorbs the clustering under test",
  "Significance", "MAD and DCLF global tests", "pointwise envelopes alone: inflate type-I error",
  "Simulations", glue("{SO$nsim} for envelopes, {ST$nperm} for Knox"), "fewer: coarse Monte Carlo p-value floor"
) |> kable()

Two of these are worth explaining properly.

Border versus Ripley correction. Ripley’s isotropic correction is more efficient but costs a lot more computation, and my envelope procedure needs 199 re-computations of it. At 10,321 points the efficiency I lose with the border correction does not matter, because the number of pairs contributing at each lag is already very large. So this is a compute trade-off and I made it deliberately rather than by accepting a default.

Global versus pointwise tests. This one took me a while to get straight. A pointwise envelope gets read at every one of several hundred values of \(r\), so the probability of at least one excursion under the null is far above the nominal level. I still plot the pointwise envelopes, because they show me where on the \(r\) axis the departure sits and a single p-value cannot. But every claim of significance I make in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

6 First-order analysis: where, and when

6.1 The pattern in its region

code

first_seen <- P$ppp_cell

6.3 Quadrat counts, and why I do not lean on them

code 
FO$quad_summary |> transmute(
  Grid = glue("{nx} x {ny}"), Quadrats = n_quadrats,
  `chi-squared` = fmt_n(round(X2)), df = df,
  VMR = vmr, `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1))) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")

My chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of magnitude at every resolution I tried, and the variance-to-mean ratio runs from 79.2 to 1036.1 against a null value of 1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.

I report this for transparency and it should persuade nobody of anything, including me. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process I described in Section 1.1, and also by the obvious geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and half comparatively intact landscape cannot possibly have uniform fire intensity. Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size, and they throw away all the within-quadrat information. The only column here I think is genuinely useful is the VMR, because it tells me how far from uniform the pattern is at each scale rather than answering a yes-or-no question I already knew the answer to.

6.4 Bandwidth selection, and why I rejected cross-validation

Kernel density estimation is the tool that actually does the work here, and the bandwidth is the decision that determines what it shows me. I spent longer on this than on any other single choice in the report.

code 
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")

Both cross-validation selectors came back with sub-kilometre bandwidths, 573 m for bw.ppl and 628 m for bw.diggle, and density.ppp threw a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over a window of 9,759 km². I did not adopt either, and it is not because the warning was inconvenient.

Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that reproduces the local bursts, so they end up treating clustering as fine-grained intensity structure. In some applications that is exactly what you want. Here it is the opposite of what I want, because I use the same estimate as the reference intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) has already soaked up the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering remains after removing \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\) is a rigged question and the answer is no by construction. I would have produced a confident and meaningless result.

So I fixed the bandwidth at 4,000 m, on a criterion I set before looking at the surfaces: it has to exceed the interaction range, so that trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of my analysis instead of competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the interaction range Section 7 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of bw.scott (3,847 m and 10,543 m), and below bw.CvL (10,530 m).

I want to be clear that this is a judgement and not an optimisation. The comparison below shows what each alternative would have given me, so anyone who disagrees can see the consequence rather than taking my word for it.

code 
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)

6.5 The intensity surface I report

code 
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +

  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))

I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

6.6 Radiative power, not just counts

A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming front as the same event, which bothered me. Fire radiative power is the sensor’s estimate of radiative output in megawatts, so smoothing that instead answers a different and arguably more useful question.

code

frpt_df <- im_df(FO$frp_total, "v") |> mutate(v = v * 1e6, panel = "Total FRP released (MW per km²)")
p1 <- ggplot(frp_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "MW") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Mean FRP per detection") + theme_map(9)
p2 <- ggplot(frpt_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, trans = "sqrt", name = "MW/km\u00b2",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Total FRP released") + theme_map(9)
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(title = "Energy release has a different geography from event count",
                          theme = theme_ex01())

7 Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness

7.1 The straw man I had to test anyway

code 
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)

7.2 What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

\(K\) and \(L\) are cumulative, which means a departure at one lag propagates into every larger lag and I cannot see where anything is actually happening. The pair correlation function \(g(r)\) is a density rather than a cumulative quantity, so it separates scales properly. This turned out to matter more than I expected.

code 
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()

7.3 The test that can fail

These are the statistics I actually trust. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything my first-order analysis established is already inside the null. If I get a departure now, it means residual interaction rather than large-scale variation, which is the question I set in Q3.

code 
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. So the pattern is clustered beyond its first-order trend, which is the answer to the first half of Q3.

What I could not establish from this was where the clustering ends, and that is down to a decision of mine that turned out to be wrong. I capped the r range at 5 km, reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. But across the whole of that range both curves sit outside the envelope, which means 5 km only establishes that dependence extends at least that far. My cap was too conservative to answer the question I had set it to answer. Section 7.5 is where I fix it.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating \(\hat{\lambda}\) from the pattern under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and makes the test harder to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

7.4 Sensitivity to the event definition

My whole analysis rests on collapsing detections to cells, so I wanted to know whether the finding depends on that choice. If it did, it would be a finding about my choice rather than about fire.

code 
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()

7.5 Extending the range, after getting it wrong

I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in Section 5 caps \(r\) at a quarter of the window’s shortest dimension, and the window is 86 km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me finally applying the rule I had already written down.

Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than hiding them. pcfinhom offers no border correction, and the translation correction over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for 99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on \(L_{inhom}\) with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of \(g_{inhom}\) comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations. I make no significance claim for \(g_{inhom}\) beyond 3 km.

code 
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
code 
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")

I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference is 0.15%, so changing the \(r\) grid has not quietly changed the estimate underneath me.

So here is my corrected answer to Q3. Residual clustering begins immediately above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly 438 m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7.2 km. My earlier statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was simply an artefact of not having looked far enough, and the conclusion I drew from it, that the first-order surface was a sufficient description above 2 km, was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag below roughly 7 km.

code 
st_df <- bind_rows(lapply(ST$st_kde, function(s)
  im_df(s$im) |> mutate(panel = format(s$date, "%d %b"))))
st_df$panel <- factor(st_df$panel, levels = vapply(ST$st_kde,
                                                   function(s) format(s$date, "%d %b"), character(1)))
ggplot(st_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = intensity / max(intensity, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.22) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Relative intensity",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fire spreads north and west from a southeastern origin") +
  theme_map(base_size = 8)

9 Value-added analysis

So far I have established that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over what distance and time the interaction operates. What I still cannot say is what the clustering is organised around, or how big a cluster actually is. Both are answerable, and both are what turn a statistical result into something an agency could act on, so I went after them.

9.1 What is the clustering organised around?

Peat fire in this landscape is overwhelmingly human in ignition and made possible by drainage. I picked two mapped covariates to proxy those mechanisms: distance to the road network, for access and ignition opportunity, and distance to mapped canals and waterways, for drainage-driven desiccation.

I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me 28,515 road features and 3,061 waterway features within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often outside the regency entirely.

The 3,061 waterway features against 28,515 road features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding. An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.

code 
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see Section 11.\n")
code 
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")

Three things in that table I want to separate out.

Distance to road does nearly all the work. My full model improves on the intercept-only model by 2,005 AIC units, and distance to road alone recovers 1,991 of them. Adding distance to water to the road model buys a further 13.4 units, which on two extra parameters is real but very small. Distance to water on its own recovers 526 units, so it is not uninformative by itself. It is mostly redundant once I know road distance, which is what I would expect if canals and tracks follow each other through the landscape.

My log specification fitted worse, not better. I included it expecting the near-field effect visible in the rhohat curve to be better captured by a log term than a linear one. It loses to the linear model on the same number of parameters, by 1,624 AIC units. Over the range of distances that actually occurs in this window, the relationship is closer to linear in distance than in its logarithm. I was wrong, and I am reporting it rather than dropping the model quietly.

None of this is causal and I want to say so plainly. Roads get built where people already work the land, so distance to road is tangled up with land use, tenure and drainage in ways my data cannot separate. The association is strong. The mechanism is not identified.

code

9.2 How large is a cluster?

A significance test tells me clustering exists. A fitted cluster process tells me how big it is, which is the form a planner could actually use. Getting that number right meant throwing away my first answer.

I first fitted a Thomas process with no trend term. It returned a cluster standard deviation of 3,292 m, about 440 events per cluster, and an implied 24 parent locations in the entire regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each across a whole regency did not sound like a cluster scale to me, and it is not. It is the southern peat belt being re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model with no trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. This is the standard identifiability problem between trend and interaction in cluster processes. If I had taken the number at face value I would have reported a confident and completely wrong operational radius.

The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides out \(\hat{\lambda}(u)\). So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function

\[g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)\]

directly to \(g_{inhom}\) by minimum contrast, minimising \(\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}\) with \(q = 1/4\) over \(r \in [200, 5,000]\) m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the fit out explicitly in R/07_cluster_scale.R rather than calling a packaged routine, because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the estimate and I wanted them visible.

code 
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
code 
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()

My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m, so about 95% of the events in a cluster fall within roughly 2,581 m of its centre, with 67 events per cluster and about 155 cluster centres across the regency. That is consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at 438 m, and I got there by a different route: minimum contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly 7.2 km not at all. A multi-scale cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it is the first thing I would try next.

9.3 Where is the single most unusual concentration?

This is the most directly practical question I ask anywhere in the report. Not whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

10.1 Consistency across approaches

My first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should and disagree in two places, and the disagreements taught me more than the agreement did.

They agree on the dominant scale. My inhomogeneous pair correlation function peaks at 438 m. My Thomas process fitted to that same curve returns a cluster standard deviation of 1,055 m. Two estimates from different machinery, one envelope-based and one model-based, both put the dominant structure at roughly a kilometre. That agreement is the main reason I am willing to quote a number.

They disagree about extent, and it is the cumulative statistic that misled me. \(L_{inhom}\) never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which tempted me to conclude that dependence extends at least that far. \(g_{inhom}\), which localises scale instead of accumulating it, shows the excess is within 10% of nothing by about 7.2 km. Both computations are correct and the second is the one I report, because \(L\) accumulates every excess at smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the range over which anything is actually happening. This is a general property of \(K\) and \(L\) rather than a quirk of my data, and it is probably the single most useful thing I learned doing this exercise.

They disagree about sufficiency, and my first-order surface loses. My earlier version, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity surface was an adequate description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong because of a decision rather than a computation: my cap was too short to see where dependence ended. Corrected, the first-order surface is not a sufficient description at any lag below roughly 7.2 km. A smooth intensity map is still a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency. It is not a tool for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has already started.

My covariate models sharpen this rather than softening it. They improve on an intercept-only model by 2,005 AIC units, so a lot of the first-order variation is explained by accessibility. But the residual \(K\) function shows they capture none of the local interaction. Location explains where fire is likely. It does not explain the contagion.

10.2 Where my analysis is weakest

Four places, roughly in order of how much they worry me.

My event definition does the heavy lifting. Collapsing detections to cells is defensible and I think necessary, but it is a modelling decision that I have presented as data preparation, and I should be honest that those are not the same thing. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass contribute identically to ppp_cell. If I weighted cells by persistence or by cumulative radiative power I would be answering a related but different question, and I am not certain I would reach the same conclusion about scale.

My inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data I am testing. The bias runs in the conservative direction, so I am comfortable that the rejection stands. But the magnitude of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated, so anything I say about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal rather than quantitative.

Detectability is confounded with intensity. I cannot discharge assumptions A1 and A2 within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode I care most about for public health, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not plausibly independent of location. What I have mapped is a surface of detected fire, not of fire.

One of my decisions was simply wrong and I had to reverse it. I initially capped the r range at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across the whole of that range, which means my cap could not answer the question I set it to answer, and my first draft drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis contradicts. I have left the cap in the record rather than quietly replacing it. A range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has no way to tell those apart unless I say which one happened.

11 Geovisualisation and geocommunication

Every figure carries its interpretation in its caption, inside the 150-word limit. This section is about the rules I gave myself for the figures themselves, because consistent encoding is what lets a reader compare one of my maps with another instead of re-learning the graphic each time.

One palette, used for one thing. I use a single warm, perceptually ordered sequential ramp for intensity in every map where intensity is the variable, and I never use it for a categorical distinction. My one diverging scale encodes a quantity that genuinely has a meaningful midpoint, the overall share of events in the peak period, and I set the midpoint to that value rather than to the middle of the data range. I kept the ramp warm even though the site’s accent colour is teal, because it is encoding fire and a teal heat map would fight its own subject.

Square-root transformation, disclosed. Fire intensity here spans roughly two orders of magnitude, so a linear ramp renders the entire regency outside the peat belt as one flat colour. I use a square-root scale so the structure of the lower range stays visible. That decision changes what a reader sees, so I label it on every scale that uses it rather than burying it.

Statistical graphics and maps share a type system. Same typeface, same rule weights, same muted axis treatment across both, because my argument moves between them continuously. I did not want a reader to experience the \(L\) function and the intensity map as coming from different documents.

Scale and orientation on every map, at minimum weight. A regency 213 km long cannot be read without a scale bar. I drew the bar and north arrow as thin line work rather than ornament, because they are reference furniture and should not compete with the data.

Uncertainty shown wherever it exists. Envelope ribbons on every second-order figure, confidence bands on the covariate curves, a normalisation note on the space-time panels. A curve drawn without its envelope invites over-reading, and over-reading is the exact failure this whole report is built to avoid.

What I deliberately left out. No three-dimensional surface: it would occlude data and add nothing a colour ramp cannot carry. No basemap imagery: it would import a visual texture I have not validated and imply a precision the 375 m grid does not support. No interpolated surface beyond the window boundary, because my analysis has no jurisdiction there.

12 Public-safety planning and management

My findings support four operational conclusions, and I have tried to keep what the evidence shows separate from what I am inferring.

Direct evidence, usable now. My intensity surface identifies where fire recurs across a season at a resolution finer than any administrative unit. Roughly two orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior. So resources allocated in proportion to sub-district area, or spread evenly, are badly matched to risk. My surface supports a concrete reallocation: concentrate standing capability in the southern third, and treat the northern interior as a response area rather than a prevention area.

Direct evidence, with a scale attached. Two methods I ran independently agree that the dominant clustering scale is about 1.1 km, with roughly 95% of a cluster’s events within 2.6 km of its centre. That gives a containment geometry I am willing to defend: when a detection arrives, the area worth immediate attention is the surrounding two to three kilometres, not the surrounding pixel and not the surrounding sub-district. Measurable elevation runs out to about 7 km, so I would treat 2.6 km as a first ring rather than a boundary. My Knox result adds the time dimension: the raised probability of a neighbouring cell igniting is concentrated in the first few days. A response window of days over a radius of kilometres is supported by what I found.

Direct evidence about monitoring, not about fire. The day and night contrast is an artefact of four fixed overpass times. Any dashboard reporting a daily fire cycle from these data would be reporting the orbit, and I nearly made that mistake myself. My pair correlation function also shows the analysis cannot resolve anything below 375 m, so these data cannot support tasking at the individual plot scale. That is a limit on the instrument. Buying a finer answer needs a different sensor, not a different statistic.

Inference that needs information I do not have. My association between intensity and proximity to roads is strong, but roads get built where land is already worked, so I cannot read it as a causal lever. Whether improving access aids suppression or enables ignition is not answerable from what I have, and the two point in opposite policy directions. Settling it needs ignition-cause records, land-tenure boundaries and enforcement data.

My flat drainage relationship is also not evidence that drainage does not matter. OpenStreetMap does not map the minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project, so my covariate is measuring mapping coverage. Testing that mechanism properly needs a canal inventory and water-table observations.

Finally, the expansion from a southeastern origin describes one season, which is all I have. Whether it recurs, and could therefore support early-season forecasting, needs the multi-year record the ninety-day retention denied me. That is the next thing I would do, and it is a data-access problem rather than a methodological one.

I fix the random seed at 626 in R/00_config.R and set it at the top of every analysis script, so all my Monte Carlo results reproduce exactly.

One engineering thing I hit that affects reproducibility in practice, and that I had not expected. spatstat’s fv and envelope objects retain the closures used to build them, and those closures capture the calling environment. Because my analysis scripts hold several multi-megabyte caches in that environment, saving the objects directly gave me an 843 MB file for extended.rds alone. I now convert each cache to plain data frames before saving, which keeps every number and brings that same file under a megabyte. The geoBoundaries download is pinned to commit 9469f09 rather than to a moving current endpoint. The FIRMS key is read from .Renviron, which is git-ignored; .Renviron.example documents what is required.

  estimation at the kilometre scale. I wanted to answer three things: where the
  detections concentrate, whether they interact beyond that concentration, and what
  a fire agency could honestly do with the answer.

  The thing that shaped the whole analysis is a distinction I nearly missed. A VIIRS
  hotspot is a 375 m pixel seen during one satellite overpass, not a fire. I measured
  the consequence: the raw detection count overstates the number of distinct burning
  locations by a factor of about 3.4. So testing the raw pattern against complete
  spatial randomness rejects the null overwhelmingly and tells me nothing, because the
  sensor guarantees that result. I switched the unit of analysis to the 375 m cell and
  the null to an inhomogeneous Poisson process, re-estimating the reference intensity
  for every simulated pattern. That gives a test that could fail. It does not.

  What I found: clustering beyond the trend is strongest at about 440 m and only
  decays to within 10% of no excess by about 7 km. That last number corrects my own
  first attempt, which capped the distance range at 5 km and concluded the excess
  stopped at 2 km. A Thomas process fitted after removing the trend puts the dominant
  cluster scale at 1.1 km, with 95% of a cluster inside 2.6 km. Fitted without
  removing the trend it returns 3.3 km and 440 events per cluster, which is really
  just the peat belt re-described as a few giant clusters. A Knox permutation test
  finds space-time interaction concentrated within a few hundred metres and a few
  days. Distance to the road network accounts for 1,991 of the 2,005 AIC units
  separating my covariate model from an intercept-only model, while mapped drainage
  accounts for almost none, which turned out to say more about OpenStreetMap coverage
  than about drainage.

# Introduction and study context

Indonesian Borneo burns every dry season, and when I started reading about it I
learned that the fires which matter most for public health are not forest fires in
the ordinary sense. They are peat fires. Drained tropical peat is a metres-deep
carbon store that, once dry, smoulders below the surface for weeks. You cannot put
it out by suppressing a surface flame front, and it releases a dense particulate
smoke that carries hundreds of kilometres. So the public-safety burden is
respiratory rather than thermal: school closures, airport closures, and a
measurable excess of acute respiratory cases across Central Kalimantan and, in bad
years, across the Malacca Strait.

Pulang Pisau Regency sits at the centre of this. Its southern half was the site of
the Mega Rice Project, a 1990s programme that cut thousands of kilometres of
drainage canal into deep peat and was then abandoned. The canals are still there,
the water table is still lowered, and the land is still unusually combustible. That
is why I did not treat the regency as just a convenient study window. It is a place
where the link between land management and public-safety outcomes is about as
visible as it gets.

Fire detections are point events in space and time, so point-pattern analysis is
the obvious tool. What I wanted to work out in this exercise is what that tool can
honestly support once you take the data seriously.

## The problem the data handed me

I need to state one thing before any analysis, because it ended up governing every
interpretation I made.

A VIIRS active-fire detection is not a fire. It is a 375 m pixel in which a
radiometer measured a thermal anomaly during a single overpass. A large peat fire
covering ten square kilometres produces many dozens of detections in one pass, and
the two satellites pass overhead roughly four times a day between them, so the same
fire gets detected over and over. What a detection actually records is *the sensor
sampling fire*, not fire occurrence. Any statistic I compute on the raw detection
set is therefore partly measuring the instrument.

Once I realised that, the textbook second-order question stopped being interesting.
"Is this pattern clustered relative to complete spatial randomness" already has a
known answer before I compute anything. It is clustered, overwhelmingly, and it
would still be clustered even if fires were sited completely at random, because
each fire produces a burst of adjacent detections. Reporting that rejection as a
finding would be close to meaningless, so I did not want to build the report on it.

Instead I changed two things, and I am stating them up front because they are the
real methodological content of this exercise rather than housekeeping. I changed
the unit of analysis from the detection to the 375 m cell, and I changed the null
model from complete spatial randomness to an inhomogeneous Poisson process.
Section 7 is where that pays off.

# Research questions and objectives

I set four questions, each with a null and a reason for asking it. I wrote these
before running the second-order analysis, so the report can be read as a test of
them rather than as a description of whatever came out.

**Q1. How does the intensity of fire detection vary across the regency, and at what
spatial scale is that variation stable?**
First-order. I ask it because a fire agency allocates fixed resources to places, so
what is useful to them is a surface, not a test. I added the scale qualifier because
a kernel estimate can be made to show almost any structure depending on the
bandwidth, so I do not think the question is answerable unless I also defend that
choice.

**Q2. How does intensity vary in time, and is the temporal signal a property of fire
activity or of the observing system?**
First-order. I split this out because the two satellites observe at fixed local
times, so any apparent daily cycle is a sampling artefact. I wanted to be sure I did
not read the orbit as fire behaviour.

**Q3. Once large-scale variation in intensity is accounted for, is there residual
interaction between events, and over what distance?**
Second-order. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson process with intensity
$\hat{\lambda}(u)$ estimated by kernel smoothing. Rejecting this null tells me
something that rejecting complete spatial randomness does not, because the
inhomogeneous null already contains everything my first-order analysis found. The
"over what distance" part is the bit with operational value, and it is also the part
I initially got wrong.

**Q4. Is there space-time interaction, over and above the separate spatial and
temporal patterns?**
Second-order, spatio-temporal. My null is random labelling: I hold the observed
locations and the observed set of dates fixed and permute only the pairing between
them. This conditions on both marginal patterns, which matters, because it means a
rejection cannot be explained away by the seasonal ramp or by the spatial
concentration. I already know both of those exist.

I added a fifth question as a value-added extension in Section 9, because the four
above tell me clustering exists without telling me what it is organised around or
how big a cluster actually is.

# Data and study design

## Sources

```{r tbl-sources}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| tbl-cap: "The data I used, as accessed. Both sources are re-creatable by running `R/01_acquire.R`. I pinned the geoBoundaries release to a commit hash so the boundary geometry cannot change underneath my analysis."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Item, ~Detail,
  "Event data", "NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m Collection 2, near-real-time (NRT)",
  "Platforms", "Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, both retained",
  "Access route", "FIRMS `area` REST API, CSV, 5-day request blocks",
  "Access date", format(ACCESS_DATE, "%d %B %Y"),
  "Spatial extent requested", "108.5 to 119.1 E, 5.2 S to 4.5 N (all Kalimantan)",
  "Boundaries", "geoBoundaries gbOpen Indonesia ADM1 and ADM2, commit 9469f09",
  "Boundary vintage", "2020, sourced from BPS Statistics Indonesia via OCHA",
  "Boundary licence", "CC BY 3.0 IGO",
  "Covariates", "OpenStreetMap via Overpass: `highway`, `waterway`",
  "Software", glue("R {getRversion()}, sf {packageVersion('sf')}, spatstat.explore {packageVersion('spatstat.explore')}")
) |> kable()
```

## Why I chose this regency

I chose the study window with a rule applied to the whole island, after downloading
data for all 56 Kalimantan regencies and cities and screening it for confidence.
The rule: **the highest detection density among regencies large enough to support
second-order estimation to a 5 km lag**, which I operationalised as an area above
5,000 km².

I used density rather than raw count because intensity relative to window area is
what governs how much signal a point pattern carries. I added the size floor because
a 5 km lag inside a small window starts to approach the window's own dimension, and
at that point edge effects dominate every second-order estimate I would compute.

```{r tbl-rank}
#| label: tbl-rank
#| tbl-cap: "The ten Kalimantan regencies with the most retained VIIRS detections, 1 July to 25 September 2026. Ketapang leads on count; Pulang Pisau leads on density among regencies above the 5,000 km² size floor, which is the selection rule applied. Kota Palangka Raya's very high density in a small window illustrates why the floor is needed."
RANK |> slice_head(n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    Regency = shapeName, Province = province,
    Detections = fmt_n(n_detections),
    `Area (km²)` = fmt_n(round(area_km2)),
    `Per 1,000 km²` = fmt_n(round(per_1000km2))
  ) |> kable(align = "llrrr")
```

Pulang Pisau wins on that rule outright, at
`r round(RANK$per_1000km2[RANK$shapeName == STUDY_REGENCY])` detections per
1,000 km². Two alternatives were seriously considered and rejected, and the
reasons are recorded because a choice is only reviewable alongside them.

**Ketapang** beat it on absolute count, with
`r fmt_n(RANK$n_detections[RANK$shapeName == "Ketapang"])` detections against Pulang
Pisau's `r fmt_n(RANK$n_detections[RANK$shapeName == STUDY_REGENCY])`. I did not
choose it because it covers
`r fmt_n(round(RANK$area_km2[RANK$shapeName == "Ketapang"]))` km², slightly over
three times the area, and ranks second on density. Its bigger count is mostly just
a bigger window.

**Kota Palangka Raya** has the highest density of any unit at
`r fmt_n(round(RANK$per_1000km2[RANK$shapeName == "Kota Palangka Raya"]))` per
1,000 km², but covers only
`r fmt_n(round(RANK$area_km2[RANK$shapeName == "Kota Palangka Raya"]))` km². A 5 km
lag there is a large fraction of the window's own width, so edge effects would drive
my second-order results rather than the fires.

Pulang Pisau also comes rank
`r which(RANK$shapeName == STUDY_REGENCY)` of `r nrow(RANK)` on raw count, so I am
not selecting some obscure unit to make the rule work. Its window of
`r fmt_n(round(P$area_km2))` km², at
`r round((bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"])/1000)` km by
`r round((bb["ymax"]-bb["ymin"])/1000)` km, comfortably supports estimation to a
5 km lag.

I should be open about how I got here. My first pass selected the regency from a
seven-day sample of the same feed, on which Pulang Pisau led on count. Over the full
87-day window it does not, Ketapang does. So I restated the selection rule against
the complete record and re-applied it. I am reporting that rather than quietly
fixing it, because a rule chosen after you have seen which unit it favours is not
really a rule, and I would rather the reader be able to judge that for themselves.

## Point event definition

I define an event as **one 375 m grid cell in which at least one qualifying VIIRS
detection was recorded**. Qualifying means all of the following, and I have given
the reason for each rather than just the rule.

```{=html}
<dl class="assump">
<dt>Sensor and product</dt>
<dd>VIIRS 375 m I-band, Collection 2, S-NPP or NOAA-20. MODIS is excluded: its
1 km footprint is coarser than the distances this analysis is about, so including
it would blur the very scale under study.</dd>
<dt>Confidence</dt>
<dd>Nominal or high. Low-confidence detections are dropped. They are dominated by
small or cool anomalies and by edge-of-scan geometry, so retaining them would
make apparent intensity vary with viewing angle rather than with fire.</dd>
<dt>Coordinates</dt>
<dd>Present, finite, within valid latitude and longitude ranges, and not the
(0, 0) sentinel that some pipelines emit for a failed geolocation.</dd>
```
