```{=html}
<dt>Timestamp</dt>
<dd>A parseable UTC acquisition time. Converted to WITA (UTC+8), because the
definition of a fire day and any reading of diurnal behaviour must be local.</dd>
<dt>Location</dt>
<dd>Strictly within the Pulang Pisau polygon. This also serves as the offshore
screen, since the polygon is terrestrial.</dd>
<dt>Not a fixed installation</dt>
<dd>See the persistence screen below. This substitutes for a field the NRT
product does not carry.</dd>
<dt>Deduplicated</dt>
<dd>Exact duplicate records removed, then collapsed to one event per 375 m cell
per local day.</dd>
</dl>
```

I build three patterns from the same screened detections, because which unit is
right depends on which question I am asking:

| Pattern | Unit | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `ppp_all` | every retained detection | sensitivity checks only |
| `ppp_daycell` | one event per 375 m cell per local day | spatio-temporal analysis |
| `ppp_cell` | one event per 375 m cell over the window | primary spatial analysis |

I use `ppp_cell` as the primary spatial pattern because it removes the
repeat-detection inflation I described in Section 1.1. A cell that burned for three
weeks and was detected eighty times contributes one point, not eighty.

For the representative point of each cell I take the earliest detection in it. That
is deterministic and it keeps a real sensor coordinate. I considered snapping to
cell centres and rejected it, because that would impose a regular lattice and
manufacture apparent regularity at small lags, which would contaminate exactly the
statistic the rest of the report depends on.

## Spatial study window

My window is the Pulang Pisau administrative polygon, unbuffered, in WGS 84 /
UTM zone 49S (EPSG:32749).

Projecting is not optional here. Every second-order statistic I use is a function of
Euclidean distance in metres, and at this latitude one degree of longitude is about
111 km while one degree of latitude is about 110.6 km. If I worked in degrees I
would be building a systematic anisotropy into every distance I compute. Zone 49S is
the right one for a regency centroid at 113.96°E, which sits inside the zone's 108°E
to 114°E span. I checked the eastern edge, which reaches 114.35°E and is marginally
outside, and the resulting scale error is below 0.1%, so it does not matter at the
kilometre scales I work at.

I used the administrative boundary rather than a buffered or natural window because
the management question is administrative: a regency fire agency has jurisdiction to
that line. The cost is a real edge effect, since fires obviously do not stop at a
boundary, and I handle it with edge correction rather than pretending it is not
there (Section 5).

## Temporal study window

**1 July to 25 September 2026, 87 days.** The lower bound was imposed on me rather
than chosen, and I want to state the constraint precisely, because it is the kind of
thing that is easy to misrepresent by accident.

```{r tbl-probe}
#| label: tbl-probe
#| tbl-cap: "Retention probe. Single-day FIRMS NRT queries over a Kalimantan-wide box. Exactly zero detections across a 10.6° by 9.7° box for every sampled date from January to 30 June is not a physically credible result for Borneo, so the zeros are read as absence of coverage. The standard-processing archive, queried for the same region in August, also returns zero rows: it has not yet been built for 2026."
PROBE$nrt |> transmute(Date = format(date, "%d %b %Y"),
                       `Detections returned` = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "lr")
```

The FIRMS `area` endpoint serves near-real-time granules on a rolling retention of
roughly 90 days, and the standard-processing archive that would have covered January
to June has not been produced for 2026. So the earliest day I can retrieve is 1 July
2026, which I located to the day with the probe above rather than assuming it. The
upper bound is my choice: the last complete UTC day before I accessed the data, so
that no partially observed day enters the daily series and shows up as a fake
decline.

I want to be careful not to oversell the window. It is what was available. But it
does happen to span the onset, escalation and peak of the 2026 dry season, which is
the period a fire agency actually acts over. If the retention limit had cut off the
peak instead of the wet-season baseline I would have had to change the study design
entirely. The honest cost is that I cannot make any wet-season comparison, so nothing
in this report speaks to the seasonal amplitude of fire activity, only to its
structure within one season. I repeat that in Section 12 because it is a real limit
on what I can claim.

## My completeness audit, and a real outage

Counting the rows I downloaded does not tell me the record is complete. The failure
mode I was worried about is a request that comes back empty, because that is
indistinguishable from a day on which nothing burned, and it would show up in my
analysis as a drop in fire activity that never happened.

So I built the audit to catch exactly that. Each of the two platforms should
contribute at least one detection somewhere in Kalimantan on every day of an 87-day
dry season, because an island-sized box is never completely without fire. Any day
where a platform contributes nothing is a candidate failure and worth chasing.

```{r tbl-gap}
#| label: tbl-gap
#| tbl-cap: "Completeness audit. Local dates on which one VIIRS platform contributed no detection anywhere in the Kalimantan bounding box. Each was re-queried four times with backoff by `R/01b_fill_gaps.R`, and each returned empty again, so these are not failed requests."
GAP$missing_after |> transmute(Date = format(dt, "%d %B %Y"),
                               `Platform absent` = platform) |> kable(align = "ll")
```

```{r}
#| label: gap-inline
#| include: false
bad <- GAP$missing_after$dt
ev_bad <- sum(P$daily_daycell$n_events[P$daily_daycell$date_local %in% bad])
ev_all <- sum(P$daily_daycell$n_events)
```

Six of the seven dates are consecutive, which made me suspect a real outage rather
than a flaky connection. Re-querying confirmed it: Suomi NPP returns an empty result
for 11 to 16 July and for 3 August no matter how many times I ask. So this is an
absence in the FIRMS near-real-time record itself, not a transient request failure I
could fix by retrying. On those seven days my analysis rests on NOAA-20 alone, and
detection counts are depressed by roughly the contribution of one platform.

The consequence is small, but I do not want to write it off as nothing. Those dates
carry
`r fmt_n(ev_bad)` of `r fmt_n(ev_all)` events, or
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * ev_bad / ev_all)` of the record, and all of them fall in
the near-zero early season before the dry-season ramp. Mean daily events on the
affected dates are `r round(mean(P$daily_daycell$n_events[P$daily_daycell$date_local %in% bad]), 1)`
against `r round(mean(P$daily_daycell$n_events[P$daily_daycell$date_local >= as.Date("2026-07-01") & P$daily_daycell$date_local <= as.Date("2026-07-26") & !(P$daily_daycell$date_local %in% bad)]), 1)`
on nearby unaffected July dates, which is consistent with losing one platform on
very small counts. No conclusion I draw turns on those seven days, but the reader
should treat the early-season part of my daily series as a slight underestimate.

# Data preparation and quality assessment

## The audit trail

I counted every exclusion. The table below is generated by the pipeline rather than
typed in by me, so it cannot drift away from what the code actually did.

```{r tbl-qa}
#| label: tbl-qa
#| tbl-cap: "My screening audit. Each row is one rule applied in `R/02_prepare.R`, in the order I applied it. Counts are rows of the detection table, before I collapse to cell-level events."
P$qa |> transmute(Step = step, Rule = rule,
                  `In` = fmt_n(n_in), Removed = fmt_n(n_removed), `Out` = fmt_n(n_out)) |>
  kable(align = "llrrr")
```

Three things I want to point out about this table.

The biggest single reduction is the spatial clip, and that is expected. I downloaded
all of Kalimantan so that I could justify my choice of regency against the
alternatives, and the overwhelming majority of those detections are outside Pulang
Pisau.

The coordinate and timestamp screens removed nothing at all. I am flagging that
rather than skipping past it, because in my experience a cleaning step that catches
nothing is often a cleaning step that is not actually testing what it says it is. I
checked mine against deliberately broken records while developing the pipeline, and
they do fire. The FIRMS product is simply well-formed here: every record had finite
coordinates in range and a parseable timestamp. I kept the screens in because I want
the pipeline to be re-runnable against other windows and products where that will
not be true.

The confidence screen removed
`r percent(P$qa$n_removed[P$qa$step == "03 confidence"] / P$qa$n_in[P$qa$step == "03 confidence"], accuracy = 0.1)`
of records, and exact duplicate removal a further
`r fmt_n(P$qa$n_removed[P$qa$step == "06 exact duplicates"])` rows, confirming
that the API does deliver a small number of repeated granule records.

```{r tbl-conf}
#| label: tbl-conf
#| tbl-cap: "Confidence classes among detections surviving the coordinate and timestamp screens, before the confidence screen itself is applied. VIIRS confidence is categorical, not a percentage."
P$conf_tab |> transmute(Confidence = confidence, Detections = fmt_n(n),
                        Share = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrr")
```

## The missing `type` field, and what I replaced it with

This was the data-quality problem that took me longest to solve. The FIRMS
standard-processing product carries a `type` field separating vegetation fire (0)
from active volcano (1), other static land source (2) and offshore (3). The NRT
product I have to use does not carry it, which I verified against the API response
header rather than assuming: `r glue("column present = {P$has_type}")`. So I had to
reconstruct the screen it would have given me.

I worked through the three cases separately:

- **Volcanoes (type 1)** are not a risk at all. Borneo has no Holocene volcano, so
  this screen is unnecessary rather than approximated. I did not need to do anything.
- **Offshore (type 3)** is already handled by my clip to the terrestrial polygon.
- **Other static land sources (type 2)** are a genuine problem. Kalimantan has
  palm-oil mills, coal operations and gas flares, and all of them show up as
  persistent thermal anomalies. This is the case I actually had to solve.

My substitute is a **persistence screen**. The logic is that a vegetation fire burns
out or moves, whereas a flare stack does not. So I score each 375 m cell by the
number of distinct local dates on which it was detected, as a fraction of the 87-day
window, and drop cells above a threshold as fixed installations.

```{r tbl-persist}
#| label: tbl-persist
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the persistence screen. The adopted threshold is 60% of days, at which the screen removes nothing. The grid extends well below that value to show where the screen would begin to act, which is the evidence that it is functional rather than merely quiet."
P$persist_sens |> transmute(
  `Threshold (share of days)` = percent(threshold, accuracy = 1),
  `Cells removed` = fmt_n(n_cells),
  `Detections removed` = fmt_n(n_detections)) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```

**My screen removed nothing.** My first reaction was that I had written it wrong, so
I checked it two ways, and I now think the empty result is correct.

First, no cell comes anywhere near the threshold. The most persistent cell in the
whole window was detected on `r P$persist_max_days` of `r P$n_days` days, which is
`r percent(P$persist_max_days / P$n_days, accuracy = 0.1)`. A flare stack or mill
would be detected on most clear-sky overpasses across the entire window, so nothing
here behaves like one.

Second, I used radiative power as an independent check, because it separates the two
cases without relying on persistence at all. A fixed industrial source emits a high
and steady radiative power, while smouldering peat emits a low one.

```{r tbl-persist-top}
#| label: tbl-persist-top
#| tbl-cap: "The ten most persistently detected cells, with their mean fire radiative power. If these were industrial sources their mean FRP would sit far above the window median; instead they sit at or near it, which is the signature of recurrent low-intensity peat combustion."
P$persist_top |> transmute(
  Cell = cell, Detections = n_det, `Days detected` = n_days,
  `Share of window` = percent(day_frac, accuracy = 0.1),
  `Mean FRP (MW)` = mean_frp) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

The median FRP across all my retained detections is `r round(P$frp_median_all, 1)`
MW, and the most persistent cells range from `r min(P$persist_top$mean_frp)` to
`r max(P$persist_top$mean_frp)` MW. They are not brighter than the population at
all. They are ordinary peat fires that happened to recur in the same cell.

That fits the regency's land use. Pulang Pisau is peatland and smallholder
agriculture, without the gas processing or open-cut coal operations that generate
persistent thermal anomalies elsewhere in Kalimantan. If I had picked a window in
East Kalimantan instead, I think this screen would have been doing real work.

I report the sensitivity across thresholds rather than a single number on purpose. If
the result swung sharply depending on where I put the line, that would be a decision
dressed up as a method, and the reader deserves to see which one it is.

## My evidence that a detection is not a fire

The claim I made in Section 1.1 is checkable, so I checked it. If detections were
independent events, most occupied cells would be detected exactly once. They are
not.

```{r fig-mult}
#| label: fig-mult
#| fig-cap: "Detections per occupied 375 m cell over the 87-day window, log scale on both axes. If each detection were an independent event, the distribution would be concentrated at one. Instead a long tail of cells is detected tens or hundreds of times, which is the repeat-observation signature of persistent fire in a fixed pixel grid observed roughly four times daily."
#| fig-height: 3.6
mt <- P$multiplicity
ggplot(mt, aes(n_det, n_cells)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = n_det, yend = 0), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.35, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_number(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Detections recorded in the cell", y = "Number of cells",
       title = "One fire, many detections",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(sum(mt$n_cells))} occupied cells. Median {median(rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells))} detections per cell, ",
                       "maximum {max(mt$n_det)}.")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

```{r}
#| label: mult-stats
#| include: false
mt_v <- rep(mt$n_det, mt$n_cells)
share_once <- mean(mt_v == 1)
infl <- P$ppp_all$n / P$ppp_cell$n
```

Only `r percent(share_once, accuracy = 0.1)` of occupied cells were detected exactly
once. The mean is `r round(mean(mt_v), 1)` detections per occupied cell, so the raw
count overstates the number of distinct burning locations by a factor of about
`r round(infl, 1)`. That is the number that convinced me. Analysing the raw
detections as a point pattern would mean analysing the satellite's revisit schedule
about as much as the fire regime, which is why I made `ppp_cell` the primary unit.

```{r tbl-patterns}
#| label: tbl-patterns
#| tbl-cap: "The three patterns I built and their mean intensities. The gap between the first and third rows is the repeat-detection inflation I quantified above."
tibble::tibble(
  Pattern = c("`ppp_all`", "`ppp_daycell`", "`ppp_cell`"),
  Unit = c("retained detection", "cell-day", "cell"),
  n = c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n),
  `Mean intensity (per 1,000 km²)` = round(c(P$ppp_all$n, P$ppp_daycell$n, P$ppp_cell$n) / P$area_km2 * 1000)
) |> mutate(n = fmt_n(n)) |> kable(align = "llrr")
```

## Geometry validation

I checked the boundary polygon for validity before using it. It is a single valid
polygon, so I did not need any multipart or self-intersection handling, though I ran
`st_make_valid` anyway as a defensive step. For point-in-polygon assignment I used
`st_within` rather than `st_intersects`, so a detection sitting exactly on the
boundary arc is excluded rather than double-counted against a neighbouring regency.
`spatstat`'s window conversion reported no points rejected as outside the window,
which tells me my clip and the `owin` agree.

Two things here commonly go wrong and I handled them deliberately. First, I assigned
regencies to parent provinces by testing containment of an interior representative
point in a projected coordinate system, not by nearest-feature matching. Nearest
feature would silently mis-assign any regency whose representative point fell
marginally outside its own province, and I would never have noticed. Second, I read
the 159 MB national ADM2 file through a bounding-box filter at the GDAL level rather
than loading it and subsetting afterwards, so the full national geometry is never
held in memory.

# Analytical assumptions and methodological decisions

Listing assumptions is easy. What I found harder, and more useful, was working out
where each one might actually fail, so I have written each with the reason I think
it could break rather than just the statement.

```{=html}
<dl class="assump">
<dt>A1. Detections are a censored observation of fire, not a sample of fires</dt>
<dd>VIIRS detects fires above a size and temperature threshold that varies with scan
angle, cloud and canopy. Smouldering sub-surface peat combustion, the dominant mode
in this landscape, is systematically under-detected because its surface signature is
weak. So what I am analysing is the pattern of <em>detectable</em> fire. That biases
against exactly the fire type I care most about for public health, and I have no
correction available within this data source. My intensity estimates are therefore a
lower bound, and their spatial variation is partly variation in detectability rather
than in fire.</dd>

<dt>A2. Cloud cover is not spatially confounded with fire location</dt>
<dd>I assume this and I cannot fully defend it. Dry-season convection over Borneo is
not spatially uniform, and smoke itself attenuates the signal. If cloud were
systematically thicker over one part of the regency, apparent intensity there would
be depressed and I would read it as less fire. I cannot establish the direction of
that bias from the detection data alone.</dd>

<dt>A3. The window is fixed and known, and events outside it are irrelevant</dt>
<dd>This is false as physics and I adopt it as a management framing. Fires cross the
regency boundary constantly. That is why I edge-correct every second-order estimate,
and why I report how sensitive my conclusions are to the correction rather than
assuming it away.</dd>

<dt>A4. The 375 m cell is the finest meaningful spatial resolution</dt>
<dd>This follows from the sensor rather than from any choice of mine. It imposes a
hard minimum separation between distinct events, and I can see it in the pair
correlation function as apparent inhibition below roughly 400 m. That inhibition is
a property of the instrument. Reading it as fires avoiding one another would be a
serious mistake, and an easy one to make.</dd>

<dt>A5. For the spatial analysis, time is collapsed</dt>
<dd>My `ppp_cell` pattern treats a cell burning in July and a cell burning in
September as the same kind of point. That is fine for "where does fire occur over a
season" and wrong for "where is fire now". I relax it in Section 8.</dd>

<dt>A6. The intensity used as the inhomogeneous null is estimable from the data</dt>
<dd>This is the weakest link in my second-order analysis and I want to be upfront
about it. Estimating $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ from the same pattern I am testing lets the
estimate absorb some of the clustering under test, which pushes the envelope outward
and makes my test conservative. I mitigate it two ways: I pick a bandwidth that
describes broad trend rather than local structure, and I re-estimate
$\hat{\lambda}$ for every simulated pattern so the data and the simulations get
identical treatment. The bias that remains pushes me toward <em>failing</em> to
detect clustering, which is why I am reasonably confident the clustering I do detect
is not an artefact of this choice.</dd>

<dt>A7. Isotropy</dt>
<dd>$K$, $L$ and $g$ all assume it, because they average over direction. I doubt it
holds here: peat fires spread with the wind and along canal lines, so I would expect
real anisotropy. Any directional structure gets averaged into a weaker isotropic
signal, so once again my reported clustering is a conservative reading rather than
an inflated one.</dd>

<dt>A8. Random labelling is the right null for space-time interaction</dt>
<dd>Permuting time labels across fixed locations conditions on both marginals. That
makes it the correct null for "is there interaction beyond the two separate
patterns" and the wrong null for "is the seasonal ramp real", which it simply
assumes. I intend that. I establish the ramp in Section 6 and I am not trying to
test it here.</dd>
</dl>
```

## My decisions, and what I rejected

```{r tbl-decisions}
#| label: tbl-decisions
#| tbl-cap: "The methodological decisions I made. The right-hand column records the alternative I considered and did not take, which I think is the part that makes a decision reviewable."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Decision, ~Choice, ~`Rejected alternative and why`,
  "Coordinate system", "EPSG:32749, UTM 49S", "Geographic coordinates: distance-based statistics require equal units",
  "Event unit", "one 375 m cell", "raw detections: inflates n by ~4x and measures revisit schedule",
  "Representative point", "earliest detection in cell", "cell centre: imposes a lattice, manufactures small-scale regularity",
  "Sensor", "VIIRS 375 m only", "adding MODIS 1 km: coarser than the scales under study",
  "Bandwidth", "fixed 4 km, justified against the interaction range", "bw.ppl and bw.diggle at ~0.6 km: absorb the clustering the second-order test is meant to detect",
  "Kernel", "Gaussian, isotropic", "quartic: negligible difference, less standard diagnostics",
  "Edge correction, KDE", "Diggle's correction", "none: 86 km-wide window, boundary understated",
  "Edge correction, K and L", "border", "Ripley isotropic: cost not justified at this n",
  "r range, K and L", "0 to 5 km", "larger: elongated window makes long lags unreliable",
  "Null model, primary", "inhomogeneous Poisson", "CSR: rejected trivially, uninformative",
  "Envelope construction", "lambda re-estimated per simulation", "fixed lambda: absorbs the clustering under test",
  "Significance", "MAD and DCLF global tests", "pointwise envelopes alone: inflate type-I error",
  "Simulations", glue("{SO$nsim} for envelopes, {ST$nperm} for Knox"), "fewer: coarse Monte Carlo p-value floor"
) |> kable()
```

Two of these are worth explaining properly.

**Border versus Ripley correction.** Ripley's isotropic correction is more efficient
but costs a lot more computation, and my envelope procedure needs `r SO$nsim`
re-computations of it. At `r fmt_n(SO$n_cell)` points the efficiency I lose with the
border correction does not matter, because the number of pairs contributing at each
lag is already very large. So this is a compute trade-off and I made it deliberately
rather than by accepting a default.

**Global versus pointwise tests.** This one took me a while to get straight. A
pointwise envelope gets read at every one of several hundred values of $r$, so the
probability of at least one excursion under the null is far above the nominal level.
I still plot the pointwise envelopes, because they show me *where* on the $r$ axis
the departure sits and a single p-value cannot. But every claim of significance I
make in this report is backed by the MAD or DCLF global test, not by the band.

# First-order analysis: where, and when

## The pattern in its region

```{r fig-context}
#| label: fig-context
#| fig-cap: "Detection density across the 56 regencies and cities of Indonesian Borneo, 1 July to 25 September 2026, with Pulang Pisau outlined. The concentration in the southern peat belt of Central Kalimantan is the regional structure within which the study window sits. What I take from it: the choice of study window is not an outlier hunt. Pulang Pisau is the most intense cell of a coherent regional band running along the southern coastal peat domes, so findings about its internal structure plausibly transfer to its neighbours. The map also shows what the regency boundary does analytically: it cuts a continuous field of fire activity, which is why the edge corrections of Section 5 matter rather than being a formality."
#| fig-height: 5.2
kal <- readRDS(file.path(DIR_DERIVED, "kal_adm2.rds")) |> st_transform(STUDY_CRS)
kal_m <- kal |> left_join(RANK |> select(shapeName, per_1000km2), by = "shapeName") |>
  mutate(per_1000km2 = tidyr::replace_na(per_1000km2, 0))
ggplot(kal_m) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = per_1000km2), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.18) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_intensity(name = "Detections per 1,000 km\u00b2", v = kal_m$per_1000km2) +
  annotate("text", x = bb["xmax"] + 60000, y = (bb["ymin"] + bb["ymax"]) / 2,
           label = "Pulang Pisau", hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = PAL$ink,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  annotate("segment", x = bb["xmax"] + 55000, xend = bb["xmax"] + 4000,
           y = (bb["ymin"] + bb["ymax"]) / 2, yend = (bb["ymin"] + bb["ymax"]) / 2,
           colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "A regional band, not an isolated hotspot") +
  theme_map() + theme(plot.margin = margin(5, 90, 5, 5))
```

## The point pattern

```{r fig-points}
#| label: fig-points
#| fig-cap: "The primary spatial pattern: one point per 375 m cell in which fire was detected. Colour shows the local date of first detection, so the map carries the season as well as the location. What I take from it: two things are immediately visible and both matter. The pattern is strongly concentrated in the southern two-thirds of the regency, which is the drained peat of the former Mega Rice Project, while the northern interior is nearly empty. Second, the colour gradient is not spatially random: earlier detections (lighter) sit disproportionately in the south and east, later ones spread north and west. That is a testable claim about space-time interaction rather than an impression, and Section 8 tests it."
#| fig-height: 6.4
pts_df <- P$fires |> st_coordinates() |> as.data.frame() |>
  bind_cols(P$fires |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(date_local))
first_seen <- P$ppp_cell
pc <- tibble(x = first_seen$x, y = first_seen$y,
             date = marks(first_seen)$date_local)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = PAL$ground_alt, colour = NA) +
  geom_point(data = pc, aes(x, y, colour = as.numeric(date - WINDOW_START) + 1),
             size = 0.16, alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours = c("#F6DFC8", "#E2803C", "#C2410C", "#4A1403"),
                         name = "Day of window (1 July = 1)",
                         breaks = c(1, 30, 60, 87)) +
  gg_win +
  labs(title = glue("{fmt_n(P$ppp_cell$n)} burned cells, coloured by first detection"))
```

## Quadrat counts, and why I do not lean on them

```{r tbl-quad}
#| label: tbl-quad
#| tbl-cap: "Chi-squared test of a homogeneous Poisson process, across quadrat resolutions. The variance-to-mean ratio (VMR) is 1 under complete spatial randomness. The verdict is identical at every resolution, which is the point: the test is not informative, it is merely arithmetically certain."
FO$quad_summary |> transmute(
  Grid = glue("{nx} x {ny}"), Quadrats = n_quadrats,
  `chi-squared` = fmt_n(round(X2)), df = df,
  VMR = vmr, `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1))) |> kable(align = "lrrrrr")
```

My chi-squared statistic exceeds its degrees of freedom by three to four orders of
magnitude at every resolution I tried, and the variance-to-mean ratio runs from
`r min(FO$quad_summary$vmr)` to `r max(FO$quad_summary$vmr)` against a null value of
1. Complete spatial homogeneity is rejected with certainty.

I report this for transparency and it should persuade nobody of anything, including
me. The result was guaranteed by the data-generating process I described in Section
1.1, and also by the obvious geography: a regency that is half drained peatland and
half comparatively intact landscape cannot possibly have uniform fire intensity.
Quadrat counts also inherit an arbitrary origin and cell size, and they throw away
all the within-quadrat information. The only column here I think is genuinely useful
is the VMR, because it tells me *how far* from uniform the pattern is at each scale
rather than answering a yes-or-no question I already knew the answer to.

## Bandwidth selection, and why I rejected cross-validation

Kernel density estimation is the tool that actually does the work here, and the
bandwidth is the decision that determines what it shows me. I spent longer on this
than on any other single choice in the report.

```{r tbl-bw}
#| label: tbl-bw
#| tbl-cap: "Bandwidth selectors compared on the primary pattern, ordered as computed. The spread is a factor of roughly eighteen from smallest to largest, which is why reporting a single surface without this table would conceal the most consequential choice in the first-order analysis."
FO$bw_tab |> transmute(Selector = selector, `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
                       `sigma (km)` = sigma_km) |> kable(align = "lrr")
```

Both cross-validation selectors came back with sub-kilometre bandwidths,
`r round(FO$sigma_ppl)` m for `bw.ppl` and `r round(FO$sigma_diggle)` m for
`bw.diggle`, and `density.ppp` threw a numerical-underflow warning at that scale over
a window of `r fmt_n(round(P$area_km2))` km². I did not adopt either, and it is not
because the warning was inconvenient.

Cross-validation selectors are documented to choose very small bandwidths when a
pattern is strongly clustered at short range. Their criteria reward a surface that
reproduces the local bursts, so they end up treating clustering as fine-grained
intensity structure. In some applications that is exactly what you want. Here it is
the opposite of what I want, because I use the same estimate as the reference
intensity for the second-order test in Section 7.3. If $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ has
already soaked up the sub-kilometre clustering, then asking whether clustering
remains after removing $\hat{\lambda}(u)$ is a rigged question and the answer is no
by construction. I would have produced a confident and meaningless result.

So I fixed the bandwidth at **`r fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)` m**, on a criterion I set
before looking at the surfaces: it has to exceed the interaction range, so that
trend and interaction are estimated by separate parts of my analysis instead of
competing for the same signal. Four kilometres sits above the interaction range
Section 7 goes on to find, inside the interval spanned by the two components of
`bw.scott` (`r fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))` m and
`r fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[2]))` m), and below `bw.CvL`
(`r fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))` m).

I want to be clear that this is a judgement and not an optimisation. The comparison
below shows what each alternative would have given me, so anyone who disagrees can
see the consequence rather than taking my word for it.

```{r fig-bw}
#| label: fig-bw
#| fig-cap: "The same pattern under four bandwidths. What I take from it: the choice is not cosmetic. The cross-validated surface resolves individual fire complexes and, at this sample size, a great deal of structure no agency could act on; it is also the surface that would sabotage the second-order test, for the reason given above. The 10.5 km bw.CvL surface is stable but has smoothed away the distinction between the peat belt and its margins, which is the distinction of interest. The adopted 4 km surface and bw.scott's 3.8 km are visually close, which is reassurance that the adopted value is not an idiosyncratic pick. What I should disclose is that all four agree on where the principal concentration is and disagree on how many secondary ones exist, so I make no claim about secondary hotspots."
#| fig-height: 5.6
bw_panels <- list(
  ppl   = glue("bw.ppl, {round(FO$sigma_ppl)} m (rejected)"),
  main  = glue("adopted, {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m"),
  scott = glue("bw.scott x, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_scott[1]))} m"),
  CvL   = glue("bw.CvL, {fmt_n(round(FO$sigma_CvL))} m"))
bw_df <- bind_rows(lapply(names(bw_panels), function(k)
  im_df(FO$kde[[k]]) |> mutate(panel = bw_panels[[k]]))) |>
  mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
bw_df$panel <- factor(bw_df$panel, levels = unlist(bw_panels))
ggplot(bw_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = bw_df$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "What the bandwidth decides") +
  theme_map(base_size = 9)
```

## The intensity surface I report

```{r fig-kde}
#| label: fig-kde
#| fig-width: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "Estimated first-order intensity of burned cells, Gaussian kernel with Diggle's edge correction, at the adopted 4 km bandwidth. What I take from it: intensity is organised as a broad south-southeast band reaching a maximum in the lower third of the regency, with a secondary extension along the eastern margin. The empty northern interior is a real absence rather than an absence of observation: the same satellites observed it on the same days. The gradient is steep, spanning roughly two orders of magnitude between the peat belt and the northern interior, which means resource allocation proportional to intensity would be very unevenly distributed. That is the operational content of a first-order surface, and it is the strongest planning-relevant thing my first-order analysis alone supports."
#| fig-height: 6.6
kde_main <- im_df(FO$kde$main) |> mutate(v = per_1000km2(intensity))
ggplot(kde_main) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_intensity(v = kde_main$v) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Fire intensity concentrates in the drained southern peat",
       subtitle = glue("Kernel intensity estimate, sigma = {fmt_n(FO$sigma_main)} m, Diggle edge correction")) +
  theme_map() + theme(legend.position = "right", legend.key.height = unit(34, "pt"),
                      legend.key.width = unit(9, "pt"))
```

I also computed an adaptive estimator as a check, because a fixed bandwidth
over-smooths sparse areas and under-smooths dense ones. It reproduces the same
principal concentration, which is the reassurance I was after: the structure I
report is not an artefact of forcing one bandwidth everywhere.

## Radiative power, not just counts

A count surface treats a barely detectable smouldering pixel and an intense flaming
front as the same event, which bothered me. Fire radiative power is the sensor's
estimate of radiative output in megawatts, so smoothing that instead answers a
different and arguably more useful question.

```{r fig-frp}
#| label: fig-frp
#| fig-cap: "Left, mean fire radiative power per detection. Right, total radiative power released, which is intensity and mean power combined. What I take from it: the two panels separate two things a single count map conflates. Total power (right) closely tracks detection intensity, so the southern peat belt dominates energy release as well as event count. Mean power per detection (left) has a different geography: it is comparatively low across the core of the peat belt and higher on the margins and in the sparse north. That is consistent with the physical expectation that peat combustion is low-intensity and persistent while fires on mineral soil and in cleared vegetation burn hotter and shorter. It is also a caution to me: the places with the most detections are not the places with the most intense individual fires."
#| fig-height: 5.8
frp_df  <- im_df(FO$frp_smooth, "v") |> mutate(panel = "Mean FRP per detection (MW)")
frpt_df <- im_df(FO$frp_total, "v") |> mutate(v = v * 1e6, panel = "Total FRP released (MW per km²)")
p1 <- ggplot(frp_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "MW") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Mean FRP per detection") + theme_map(9)
p2 <- ggplot(frpt_df) + geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = v)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, trans = "sqrt", name = "MW/km\u00b2",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + labs(subtitle = "Total FRP released") + theme_map(9)
p1 + p2 + plot_annotation(title = "Energy release has a different geography from event count",
                          theme = theme_ex01())
```

## Temporal intensity

```{r fig-daily}
#| label: fig-daily
#| fig-cap: "Daily count of burned cells with a centred seven-day mean, and the onset/peak split used later. What I take from it: the episode is not a plateau. Activity is negligible through early July, rises from late July, and escalates sharply through August to a maximum in the first half of September. The seven-day mean is shown because the raw series carries strong short-period structure from cloud cover and overpass geometry, not from fire: a single overcast day suppresses detection regardless of what is burning. I placed the split date by a rule I set in advance, the first day the seven-day mean reaches half its eventual maximum, rather than choosing it after seeing the surfaces I later use it to compare."
#| fig-height: 3.8
dsplit <- ST$split_date
ggplot(FO$daily, aes(date_local)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = n_events), fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 0.85) +
  geom_line(aes(y = roll7), colour = PAL$accent_dk, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(dsplit), colour = PAL$cool,
             linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = dsplit, y = max(FO$daily$n_events) * 0.96,
           label = glue(" onset | peak split, {format(dsplit, '%d %b')}"),
           hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 weeks", date_labels = "%d %b") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Burned cells per day",
       title = "A season that escalates, not a steady state",
       subtitle = "Bars, daily count of 375 m cells newly detected. Line, centred seven-day mean.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

```{r fig-overpass}
#| label: fig-overpass
#| fig-cap: "Detections by local solar time of acquisition, split by platform. What I take from it: I put this figure in to stop myself making a mistake. The two platforms observe at four narrow fixed local times, so the apparent day and night counts are not a diurnal cycle of fire activity; they are two sampling windows. Peat fires smoulder continuously and their true diurnal variation cannot be recovered from these data at all. If I said 'fires peak in the early afternoon' I would be describing the satellite's orbit, not the fires. I use the day and night split only as a detectability covariate, since night overpasses catch cooler anomalies against a cooler background."
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(FO$overpass, aes(hr_bin, n, fill = daynight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.42) +
  facet_wrap(~platform, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(day = PAL$accent, night = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = "Local solar time (WITA, UTC+8)", y = "Detections",
       title = "Four fixed overpasses, not a diurnal cycle") +
  theme_ex01()
```

# Second-order analysis: clustering, inhibition, or randomness

## The straw man I had to test anyway

```{r fig-csr}
#| label: fig-csr
#| fig-cap: "Nearest-neighbour G, empty-space F, and the centred L function, each against a complete spatial randomness envelope from 199 simulations. What I take from it: every statistic departs from the CSR envelope immediately and by an enormous margin. G rises far faster than expected, meaning nearest neighbours are much closer than random; F rises far slower, meaning empty gaps are much larger than random; L sits far above zero at every lag. Read naively this is overwhelming evidence of clustering. Read correctly it is evidence of almost nothing, because the sensor guarantees this result: a single fire produces adjacent detections. I include it to make that failure visible rather than hide it. The analysis I actually rely on is in Section 7.3."
#| fig-height: 3.4
mk_env_df <- function(e, lab) e |> mutate(panel = lab)
eg <- mk_env_df(SO$env_G, "G(r), nearest neighbour")
ef <- mk_env_df(SO$env_F, "F(r), empty space")
el <- SO$env_L |>
  mutate(across(c(obs, theo, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), panel = "L(r) - r, centred")
env_all <- bind_rows(eg, ef, el)
env_all$panel <- factor(env_all$panel, levels = c("G(r), nearest neighbour",
                                                  "F(r), empty space", "L(r) - r, centred"))
ggplot(env_all, aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = theo), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Against complete spatial randomness, everything is significant",
       subtitle = glue("Orange, observed. Grey band, envelope from {SO$nsim} CSR simulations. Dashed, theoretical CSR value.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

## What the pair correlation function reveals about the instrument

$K$ and $L$ are cumulative, which means a departure at one lag propagates into every
larger lag and I cannot see where anything is actually happening. The pair
correlation function $g(r)$ is a density rather than a cumulative quantity, so it
separates scales properly. This turned out to matter more than I expected.

```{r fig-pcf}
#| label: fig-pcf
#| fig-cap: "Pair correlation function of the primary pattern, log scale. The dotted line marks the 375 m VIIRS pixel dimension. What I take from it: g(r) is suppressed at very short range and peaks at about 460 m, immediately above the pixel width. This is not fires avoiding one another. It is the sensor's resolution: two detections cannot be much closer than one pixel, because one pixel yields one detection. That short-range suppression is an instrument artefact and is the clearest single piece of evidence that this pattern records observation rather than events. Above the peak, g(r) decays slowly and is still above 3 at 2.9 km, nowhere near its asymptote of 1. So spatial dependence extends well beyond the 5 km range I plot here, which is what pushed me to Section 7.5."
#| fig-height: 3.6
pcf_df <- SO$pcf_obs |> filter(is.finite(trans), r > 0)
ggplot(pcf_df, aes(r, trans)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = DEDUP_GRID_M, colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = DEDUP_GRID_M + 60, y = max(pcf_df$trans) * 0.85,
           label = "375 m pixel", hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = PAL$cool,
           family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "The sensor's footprint is visible in the statistic",
       subtitle = "Suppression below one pixel width is an instrument property, not fire behaviour.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

## The test that can fail

These are the statistics I actually trust. My null is an inhomogeneous Poisson
process whose intensity is the kernel estimate from Section 6.5, so everything my
first-order analysis established is already inside the null. If I get a departure
now, it means residual interaction rather than large-scale variation, which is the
question I set in Q3.

```{r fig-inhom}
#| label: fig-inhom
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function and inhomogeneous pair correlation function, against envelopes from 199 simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process. The reference intensity is re-estimated for every simulated pattern. What I take from it: the departure survives, and it does not close. Both curves leave the envelope at about 100 m and remain outside it across the entire range plotted. g_inhom peaks near 5.9 at roughly 570 m and is still above 2 at 2.8 km, against an envelope ceiling near 1.4. So after accounting for the fact that fire is far more likely in the southern peat belt than in the north, burned cells still occur much closer together than that variation alone predicts. Note also that g_inhom falls below 1 at the shortest lags, the sensor floor surviving into the inhomogeneous statistic."
#| fig-height: 3.6
# An envelope built from `simulate=` has no theoretical curve, only the simulation
# mean, so the reference is set explicitly: 0 for the centred L function and 1 for
# the pair correlation function.
li <- SO$env_Linhom |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r),
                              ref = 0, panel = "L_inhom(r) - r")
gi <- SO$env_pcfinhom |> filter(r > 0) |> mutate(ref = 1, panel = "g_inhom(r)")
ggplot(bind_rows(li, gi), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Clustering survives the honest null, and has a scale",
       subtitle = glue("Envelope from {SO$nsim} simulations of an inhomogeneous Poisson process with lambda re-estimated each time.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-global}
#| label: tbl-global
#| tbl-cap: "Global Monte Carlo tests. The maximum absolute deviation (MAD) and Diggle-Cressie-Loosmore-Ford (DCLF) statistics each summarise the whole curve in one number, so these p-values are not inflated by reading a band at many lags. The Monte Carlo floor is 0.01 with 99 simulations."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Test, ~Statistic, ~Null, ~`p-value`,
  "MAD",  "L(r)",       "complete spatial randomness",  fmt_p(SO$mad_L$p.value, 99),
  "MAD",  "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$mad_Linhom$p.value, 99),
  "DCLF", "L_inhom(r)", "inhomogeneous Poisson",        fmt_p(SO$dclf_Linhom$p.value, 99)
) |> kable(align = "lllr")
```

Both global tests reject the inhomogeneous Poisson null at the Monte Carlo floor. So
the pattern is clustered **beyond** its first-order trend, which is the answer to the
first half of Q3.

What I could not establish from this was where the clustering ends, and that is down
to a decision of mine that turned out to be wrong. I capped the r range at 5 km,
reasoning that longer lags in an elongated window rest on too few pairs. But across
the whole of that range both curves sit outside the envelope, which means 5 km only
establishes that dependence extends *at least* that far. My cap was too conservative
to answer the question I had set it to answer. Section 7.5 is where I fix it.

The direction of the remaining bias matters for how confidently this can be
stated. As set out in assumption A6, estimating $\hat{\lambda}$ from the pattern
under test lets it absorb part of the clustering, which widens the envelope and
makes the test *harder* to reject. The rejection therefore stands despite a
conservative procedure, not because of a permissive one.

## Sensitivity to the event definition

My whole analysis rests on collapsing detections to cells, so I wanted to know
whether the finding depends on that choice. If it did, it would be a finding about
my choice rather than about fire.

```{r fig-sens}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Inhomogeneous centred L function computed on the cell pattern and on the un-thinned detection pattern, on a common axis. What I take from it: both curves are positive, so the qualitative conclusion of residual clustering does not depend on the event definition. The magnitudes differ by roughly an order of magnitude, and the un-thinned pattern shows far stronger apparent clustering at every lag. That gap is the repeat-detection artefact measured directly. It is why I use the cell pattern for inference and the detection pattern only for this check. If I reported the upper curve I would be reporting the satellite revisit schedule as a fire-behaviour result."
#| fig-height: 3.4
sd_df <- bind_rows(
  SO$Linhom_cell |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_cell (reported)"),
  SO$Linhom_all  |> transmute(r, v = border - r, pattern = "ppp_all (un-thinned)"))
ggplot(sd_df, aes(r, v, colour = pattern)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("ppp_cell (reported)" = PAL$accent,
                                 "ppp_all (un-thinned)" = PAL$cool), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = "L_inhom(r) - r",
       title = "The conclusion is robust, the magnitude is not",
       subtitle = glue("n = {fmt_n(SO$n_cell)} cells against n = {fmt_n(SO$n_all)} detections.")) +
  theme_ex01()
```

## Extending the range, after getting it wrong

I set the 5 km cap because long lags in an elongated window rest on few pairs. That
reasoning is fine, but 5 km was more conservative than I needed. The rule I stated in
Section 5 caps $r$ at a quarter of the window's shortest dimension, and the window is
`r round((bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"])/1000)` km wide, so 20 km was admissible the whole
time. Extending to 20 km is not me granting myself a post-hoc licence, it is me
finally applying the rule I had already written down.

Two practical constraints came with that, and I am disclosing both rather than
hiding them. `pcfinhom` offers no border correction, and the translation correction
over roughly seven million pairs per pattern would not finish in a workable time for
99 simulated patterns. So my significance across the extended range rests on
$L_{inhom}$ with a border correction and a full envelope, while the shape of
$g_{inhom}$ comes from a single translation-corrected curve with no simulations.
**I make no significance claim for $g_{inhom}$ beyond 3 km.**

```{r fig-ext}
#| label: fig-ext
#| fig-cap: "Left, inhomogeneous centred L function to 20 km with a 99-simulation envelope. Right, the observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function over the same range, with no envelope, on a log scale. What I take from it: the two panels answer different questions and disagree in an instructive way. g_inhom, which localises scale, peaks at about 440 m and decays steadily: it is 4.3 at 1 km, 2.7 at 2 km, 1.4 at 5 km, and reaches within 10% of its asymptote of 1 at about 7.2 km. L_inhom, which is cumulative, never re-enters its envelope within 20 km. Both are correct. The excess pair density is a local phenomenon that has largely dissipated by 7 km, and because L accumulates every excess at smaller lags it remains significantly elevated far beyond the range over which anything is actually happening."
#| fig-height: 3.6
Lx <- EX$env_L_ext |> mutate(across(c(obs, lo, hi), ~ .x - r), ref = 0,
                             panel = "L_inhom(r) - r, with envelope")
Gx <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, is.finite(trans)) |>
  transmute(r, obs = trans, lo = NA_real_, hi = NA_real_, ref = 1,
            panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only")
ggplot(bind_rows(Lx, Gx), aes(r)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ref), colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(aes(y = obs), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(panel = "g_inhom(r), observed only",
                           x = EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1),
             aes(xintercept = x), colour = PAL$cool, linetype = "12", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  labs(x = "r", y = NULL,
       title = "Dependence is local, but a cumulative statistic cannot say so",
       subtitle = glue("Dotted line marks {round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)} km, where g_inhom first comes within 10% of 1.")) +
  theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
```

```{r tbl-ext}
#| label: tbl-ext
#| tbl-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation at selected lags. A value of 1 means no excess over the inhomogeneous Poisson expectation."
with(EX$summary_ext, tibble::tibble(
  Lag = c("peak", "1 km", "2 km", "5 km", "10 km", "20 km"),
  `g_inhom` = round(c(peak_g, g_1km, g_2km, g_5km, g_10km, g_20km), 2),
  Note = c(glue("at {round(peak_r_m)} m"), "", "", "", "", "sampling noise at this lag")
)) |> kable(align = "lrl")
```

```{r}
#| label: ext-crosscheck
#| include: false
cc <- EX$correction_cmp
cc_med <- 100 * median(abs(cc$rel_diff), na.rm = TRUE)
```

I cross-checked the extended curve against my Section 7.3 estimate over the lags
both cover, since both use the translation correction. The median relative difference
is `r sprintf("%.2f%%", cc_med)`, so changing the $r$ grid has not quietly changed
the estimate underneath me.

**So here is my corrected answer to Q3.** Residual clustering begins immediately
above the sensor floor, is strongest at roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and only decays to within 10% of no excess by
about `r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. My earlier
statement that the excess was exhausted by 2 km was simply an artefact of not having
looked far enough, and the conclusion I drew from it, that the first-order surface
was a sufficient description above 2 km, was wrong. It is not sufficient at any lag
below roughly 7 km.

# Spatio-temporal analysis

## Space-time interaction

```{r tbl-knox}
#| label: tbl-knox
#| tbl-cap: "Knox test of space-time interaction across a grid of spatial and temporal thresholds. Each cell counts observed pairs close in both space and time, against the mean under 999 random labellings in which locations and dates are held fixed and only their pairing is permuted. The ratio is observed over expected."
ST$knox_tab |> transmute(
  `Space (m)` = fmt_n(s_m), `Time (days)` = t_days,
  Observed = fmt_n(observed), `Expected` = fmt_n(round(exp_perm)),
  Ratio = round(ratio, 2),
  `p-value` = vapply(p_value, fmt_p, character(1), nperm = ST$nperm)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrr")
```

```{r fig-knox}
#| label: fig-knox
#| fig-cap: "Knox ratio of observed to expected close pairs, by spatial and temporal threshold. What I take from it: interaction is strongest in the tightest cell, pairs within a few hundred metres and one day, and decays monotonically as either threshold widens. That shape is the signature of local, short-lived propagation: a cell that burns today makes a neighbouring cell more likely to burn tomorrow, and the effect is largely spent within a few days and a kilometre or two. The decay in the time direction is steeper than in the space direction, which is consistent with fires spreading over contiguous ground within days rather than recurring in the same place weeks apart. Because the null holds both marginals fixed, none of this can be attributed to the seasonal escalation shown in Figure 8."
#| fig-height: 3.6
ggplot(ST$knox_tab, aes(factor(s_m), factor(t_days), fill = ratio)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", ratio)), size = 3.1, colour = PAL$ink,
            family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Observed / expected") +
  labs(x = "Spatial threshold (m)", y = "Temporal threshold (days)",
       title = "Interaction is local in space and short in time",
       subtitle = glue("{fmt_n(ST$n_close_pairs)} close pairs, {ST$nperm} random labellings.")) +
  theme_ex01(grid = "none")
```

## Does the signature move between onset and peak?

```{r fig-rr}
#| label: fig-rr
#| fig-cap: "Probability that a burned cell belongs to the peak period rather than the onset period, as a spatially varying surface. Values above the overall peak share indicate areas where fire arrived late; values below indicate areas that burned early. What I take from it: the surface is not flat, so the episode is not a uniform intensification of one fixed footprint. The southern and southeastern peat burned disproportionately early, while the northern and western margins of the active area contribute disproportionately to the peak period. Read together with the trajectory in the next figure, this describes an episode that begins in the most degraded peat and expands outward from it. The operational implication I draw is that where fire is early in the season carries information about where it will appear later, which my static seasonal intensity map cannot convey."
#| fig-height: 6.2
rr_df <- im_df(ST$rr, "p")
share_peak <- as.numeric(ST$season_counts["peak"]) / sum(ST$season_counts)
ggplot(rr_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = p)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = PAL$cool, mid = PAL$ground_alt, high = PAL$accent_dk,
                       midpoint = share_peak, name = "P(peak period)",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "The episode expands rather than intensifies in place",
       subtitle = glue("Split at {format(ST$split_date, '%d %B')}. Midpoint of the scale is the overall peak share, {percent(share_peak, accuracy = 1)}.")) +
  theme_map()
```

```{r fig-traj}
#| label: fig-traj
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean centre of burned cells with the weekly dispersion about it, and the distance the centre moved each week. What I take from it: the mean centre is a crude summary and I use it only for what it does reliably, which is showing direction and spread over time. Dispersion widens as the season progresses, which confirms the expansion I read off the relative-risk surface. The weekly displacement of the centre is largest in the early weeks, when few cells dominate the mean, and settles to a few kilometres a week once activity is widespread. The caution I would attach is that the mean centre of a strongly non-convex, multi-modal pattern is not a place where anything is happening. It is a summary statistic and I would not put it on an operational map."
#| fig-height: 3.6
tr <- ST$traj |> filter(n > 0)
p_sd <- ggplot(tr, aes(week_start, sd_km)) +
  geom_col(fill = PAL$accent_lt, width = 4.4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Standard distance (km)", subtitle = "Dispersion of burned cells") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_step <- ggplot(tr |> filter(!is.na(step_km)), aes(week_start, step_km)) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL$accent_dk, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL$accent_dk, size = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekly shift of mean centre (km)", subtitle = "Movement of the mean centre") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b") + theme_ex01()
p_sd + p_step + plot_annotation(
  title = "The footprint widens as the season progresses", theme = theme_ex01())
```

## Space-time intensity

```{r fig-st}
#| label: fig-st
#| fig-cap: "Space-time intensity at fortnightly reference days, estimated with a fixed spatial kernel and a Gaussian weight in time of five days' standard deviation. Each panel is normalised to its own weights, so panels show where fire was concentrated at that moment rather than how much there was. What I take from it: the sequence makes the expansion explicit. Early July activity is confined to a small southeastern area. Through August the active area extends north and west along the peat belt while retaining the southern core. By mid-September activity covers most of the southern two-thirds of the regency. My estimator assumes separability, meaning the spatial kernel does not change shape over time. That is a simplification: the real footprint is elongating, and a separable estimator can only show that as a change in weights."
#| fig-height: 4.4
st_df <- bind_rows(lapply(ST$st_kde, function(s)
  im_df(s$im) |> mutate(panel = format(s$date, "%d %b"))))
st_df$panel <- factor(st_df$panel, levels = vapply(ST$st_kde,
                                                   function(s) format(s$date, "%d %b"), character(1)))
ggplot(st_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = intensity / max(intensity, na.rm = TRUE))) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.22) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Relative intensity",
                       labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1)) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Fire spreads north and west from a southeastern origin") +
  theme_map(base_size = 8)
```

# Value-added analysis

So far I have established that fire is clustered, where it concentrates, and over
what distance and time the interaction operates. What I still cannot say is what the
clustering is organised around, or how big a cluster actually is. Both are
answerable, and both are what turn a statistical result into something an agency
could act on, so I went after them.

## What is the clustering organised around?

Peat fire in this landscape is overwhelmingly human in ignition and made possible by
drainage. I picked two mapped covariates to proxy those mechanisms: distance to the
road network, for access and ignition opportunity, and distance to mapped canals and
waterways, for drainage-driven desiccation.

I took the covariate geometry from a dated Geofabrik OpenStreetMap extract for
Kalimantan rather than a live Overpass query. That was not my first choice. Overpass
refused a bounding box this size repeatedly, and once I had switched I realised the
extract is better anyway: a live query returns different data every time it runs, so
it cannot be part of a reproducible pipeline. The extract gave me
`r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road features and `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway features
within a 15 km buffer of the regency.

I compute distances on that buffered frame and only then crop to the analysis
window. If I had computed them on the clipped window I would have biased every
distance upward for cells near the boundary, because their nearest road is often
outside the regency entirely.

The `r fmt_n(CM$n_water)` waterway features against `r fmt_n(CM$n_roads)` road
features is itself my first result here, and it is a warning rather than a finding.
An area defined by an abandoned canal network has fewer mapped watercourses than
roads. I come back to what that does to the drainage covariate below.

```{r fig-rho}
#| label: fig-rho
#| fig-cap: "Estimated intensity as a non-parametric function of distance to the nearest road and to the nearest mapped waterway, with 95% confidence bands. The horizontal line is the mean intensity over the window. What I take from it: intensity falls steeply with distance from a road, from well above the window mean within the first kilometre to below it beyond a few kilometres. That is a strong and monotone access effect, consistent with ignition being human. The waterway relationship is weaker and less monotone. This is my more interesting negative result. It does not show drainage is unimportant, it shows OpenStreetMap's waterway layer is a poor proxy for it, because the dense minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project is largely unmapped. My covariate is measuring mapping effort as much as hydrology, so I read the flat curve as absence of evidence."
#| fig-height: 3.6
rho_to_df <- function(rh, lab) {
  if (is.null(rh)) return(NULL)
  d <- rh
  nm <- names(d)
  tibble(x = d[[1]], rho = d[["rho"]],
         lo = if ("lo" %in% nm) d[["lo"]] else NA_real_,
         hi = if ("hi" %in% nm) d[["hi"]] else NA_real_, panel = lab)
}
rho_df <- bind_rows(
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_road,  "Distance to nearest road"),
  rho_to_df(CM$rho_water, "Distance to nearest mapped waterway"))
mean_int <- P$ppp_cell$n / (P$area_km2 * 1e6)
if (!is.null(rho_df) && nrow(rho_df)) {
  ggplot(rho_df, aes(x / 1000)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = per_1000km2(mean_int) / 1e3 * 1e3,
               colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = per_1000km2(lo), ymax = per_1000km2(hi)),
                fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_line(aes(y = per_1000km2(rho)), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Burned cells per 1,000 km²",
         title = "Access explains a great deal, mapped drainage very little",
         subtitle = "Dashed line, mean intensity over the window.") +
    theme_ex01(base_size = 9)
} else cat("Covariate estimation unavailable; see Section 11.\n")
```

```{r tbl-aic}
#| label: tbl-aic
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted Poisson point-process models compared by AIC. Distances are in kilometres, so coefficients read per kilometre. The log specification was included on the expectation that a steep near-field effect flattening with distance would fit better than a linear term; it does not, and is reported as a failed expectation rather than dropped."
CM$aic_tab |> transmute(Model = model, Parameters = npar,
                        AIC = fmt_n(round(AIC)), `Delta AIC` = fmt_n(round(dAIC))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: aic-inline
#| include: false
dn <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "null"]
dr <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
dw <- dn - CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "water"]
dboth_over_road <- CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "road"]
```

Three things in that table I want to separate out.

**Distance to road does nearly all the work.** My full model improves on the
intercept-only model by `r fmt_n(round(dn))` AIC units, and distance to road alone
recovers `r fmt_n(round(dr))` of them. Adding distance to water to the road model
buys a further `r round(dboth_over_road, 1)` units, which on two extra parameters is
real but very small. Distance to water on its own recovers `r fmt_n(round(dw))`
units, so it is not uninformative by itself. It is mostly redundant once I know road
distance, which is what I would expect if canals and tracks follow each other
through the landscape.

**My log specification fitted worse, not better.** I included it expecting the
near-field effect visible in the rhohat curve to be better captured by a log term
than a linear one. It loses to the linear model on the same number of parameters, by
`r fmt_n(round(CM$aic_tab$dAIC[CM$aic_tab$model == "log"]))` AIC units. Over the
range of distances that actually occurs in this window, the relationship is closer to
linear in distance than in its logarithm. I was wrong, and I am reporting it rather
than dropping the model quietly.

**None of this is causal and I want to say so plainly.** Roads get built where
people already work the land, so distance to road is tangled up with land use,
tenure and drainage in ways my data cannot separate. The association is strong. The
mechanism is not identified.

```{r fig-resk}
#| label: fig-resk
#| fig-cap: "Residual K function for the best-fitting Poisson model. If the fitted covariate trend fully explained the pattern, this curve would sit on zero within its envelope. What I take from it: it does not. A substantial positive residual remains at short lags, which means the covariates account for part of the first-order variation but none of the local interaction found in Section 7.3. Substantively: knowing how far a place is from a road tells me whether it is likely to burn. It does not tell me that burning is contagious at the kilometre scale. A Poisson model cannot represent contagion by construction, which is the motivation for the cluster process fitted next."
#| fig-height: 3.4
if (!is.null(CM$res_K)) {
  rk <- CM$res_K
  ycol <- if ("bres" %in% names(rk)) "bres" else names(rk)[2]
  ggplot(rk, aes(r, .data[[ycol]])) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_line(colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.7) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
    labs(x = "r", y = "Residual K",
         title = "The covariates explain location, not contagion") +
    theme_ex01()
} else cat("Residual K unavailable.\n")
```

## How large is a cluster?

A significance test tells me clustering exists. A fitted cluster process tells me how
big it is, which is the form a planner could actually use. Getting that number right
meant throwing away my first answer.

I first fitted a Thomas process with no trend term. It returned a cluster standard
deviation of `r fmt_n(round(TH$kppm_hom$sigma_m))` m, about
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$mu_per_cluster)` events per cluster, and an implied
`r round(TH$kppm_hom$kappa_per_km2 * P$area_km2)` parent locations in the entire
regency. Twenty-three clusters of 440 events each across a whole regency did not
sound like a cluster scale to me, and it is not. It is the southern peat belt being
re-described as a handful of enormous clusters, which is the only way a model with
no trend term can represent large-scale intensity variation. This is the standard
identifiability problem between trend and interaction in cluster processes. If I had
taken the number at face value I would have reported a confident and completely
wrong operational radius.

The fix is to remove the trend before estimating the cluster parameters. My
inhomogeneous pair correlation function already does exactly that, because it divides
out $\hat{\lambda}(u)$. So I fitted the Thomas pair correlation function

$$g(r) \;=\; 1 + \frac{1}{4\pi\kappa\sigma^{2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^{2}}{4\sigma^{2}}\right)$$

directly to $g_{inhom}$ by minimum contrast, minimising
$\sum_r \left(\hat{g}(r)^{q} - g_\theta(r)^{q}\right)^{2}$ with $q = 1/4$ over
$r \in [`r TH$RMIN`, `r fmt_n(TH$RMAX)`]$ m. I set the lower limit to exclude lags
governed by the 375 m sensor floor rather than by the cluster process. I wrote the
fit out explicitly in `R/07_cluster_scale.R` rather than calling a packaged routine,
because the objective function and the excluded range are the substance of the
estimate and I wanted them visible.

```{r tbl-thomas}
#| label: tbl-thomas
#| tbl-cap: "Thomas cluster process fitted by minimum contrast, with and without the first-order trend removed. sigma is the standard deviation of offspring displacement from the cluster centre and r95 the radius containing about 95% of a cluster's events. The contrast between the two rows is the finding: leaving the trend in the model inflates the estimated cluster scale by a factor of two, and the implied cluster sizes become absurd."
TH$thomas_tab |> transmute(
  Specification = spec,
  `sigma (m)` = round(sigma_m),
  `r95 (m)` = round(r95_m),
  `Parents in regency` = round(n_parents_implied),
  `Events per cluster` = round(mu_per_cluster)) |> kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| label: thomas-inline
#| include: false
tp <- TH$thomas_tab |> filter(key == "trend_removed")
r95 <- round(tp$r95_m); sig_t <- round(tp$sigma_m); mu_t <- round(tp$mu_per_cluster)
```

```{r fig-thomas}
#| label: fig-thomas
#| fig-cap: "Observed inhomogeneous pair correlation function with the two fitted Thomas models, log scale, over the range used for fitting. The shaded band marks lags below 200 m, excluded from the fit because they are governed by the sensor's pixel size. What I take from it: the trend-removed fit tracks the observed curve closely from the peak outward, which is the range that matters for an operational radius. The fit that retains the trend is too flat and too wide, because its cluster component is doing work that belongs to the intensity surface. Neither fit captures the observed curve beyond about 4 km, where the observed g_inhom decays more slowly than a single Gaussian cluster kernel allows. That is a real limitation of my model: the pattern has structure at more than one scale, and a one-scale model cannot represent it."
#| fig-height: 3.6
gobs <- EX$g_obs_ext |> filter(r > 0, r <= TH$RMAX, is.finite(trans))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = TH$RMIN, ymin = 1, ymax = max(gobs$trans) * 1.05,
           fill = PAL$rule, alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = PAL$muted, linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.35) +
  geom_line(data = gobs, aes(r, trans), colour = PAL$accent, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = TH$curves, aes(r, g, linetype = spec), colour = PAL$cool,
            linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(2, 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = " km")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "r", y = "g(r), log scale",
       title = "Removing the trend halves the estimated cluster scale",
       subtitle = "Orange, observed inhomogeneous pcf. Blue, fitted Thomas models. Shaded, lags excluded from the fit.") +
  theme_ex01()
```

My trend-removed fit gives a cluster standard deviation of `r fmt_n(sig_t)` m, so
about 95% of the events in a cluster fall within roughly `r fmt_n(r95)` m of its
centre, with `r mu_t` events per cluster and about
`r round(tp$n_parents_implied)` cluster centres across the regency. That is
consistent with my pair correlation function, which peaks at
`r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m, and I got there by a different route: minimum
contrast fitting of a mechanistic model rather than envelope testing.

Two estimates agreeing is stronger than either alone, but the agreement is only
partial and I should say where it breaks. My fitted model has a single scale, and
the figure below shows the observed curve decaying more slowly beyond about 4 km
than a single Gaussian kernel allows. So the Thomas process describes the dominant
local structure well and the longer tail of dependence out to roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km not at all. A multi-scale
cluster process, or a log-Gaussian Cox process with a flexible covariance, would be
the natural next model. Fitting one is beyond what I can do in this exercise, but it
is the first thing I would try next.

## Where is the single most unusual concentration?

This is the most directly practical question I ask anywhere in the report. Not
whether clustering exists, but where the single most unusual concentration sits and
whether it is more extreme than chance would produce.

```{r tbl-scan}
#| label: tbl-scan
#| tbl-cap: "Spatial scan statistic, Poisson model, circular windows of 2, 5 and 10 km radius, 99 Monte Carlo simulations. The location is the maximum of the likelihood-ratio surface."
sc <- CM$scan_res
lrts <- attr(sc, "obsLRTS")
w  <- which(lrts$v == max(lrts$v, na.rm = TRUE), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
mx <- c(x = lrts$xcol[w[2]], y = lrts$yrow[w[1]])
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(mx["x"], mx["y"])), crs = STUDY_CRS), 4326))
tibble::tibble(
  `Max likelihood-ratio statistic` = round(as.numeric(sc$statistic), 1),
  `p-value` = fmt_p(sc$p.value, 99),
  `Radii tested (km)` = paste(attr(sc, "r") / 1000, collapse = ", "),
  `Most likely cluster centre` = sprintf("%.3f E, %.3f S", ll[1], abs(ll[2]))
) |> kable(align = "rrll")
```

```{r fig-scan}
#| label: fig-scan
#| fig-cap: "Likelihood-ratio surface from the spatial scan statistic, with the maximum marked. What I take from it: the surface is not a second intensity map. It measures, at each location, how much better a model with an elevated rate inside a circle fits than a model with a constant rate, so it answers where I would look first rather than where fire is densest. The maximum sits in the southern peat belt, consistent with the kernel intensity estimate, and the statistic is significant at the Monte Carlo floor. What this adds over my intensity map is that it is explicitly comparative. The broad plateau shows several locations are nearly as unusual as the maximum, so I would over-read it if I treated the single peak as uniquely important."
#| fig-height: 6.2
ls_df <- im_df(lrts, "lrts")
ggplot(ls_df) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = lrts)) +
  geom_sf(data = win_p, fill = NA, colour = PAL$ink, linewidth = 0.45) +
  annotate("point", x = mx["x"], y = mx["y"], shape = 21, size = 3.4,
           colour = PAL$ink, fill = NA, stroke = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = mx["x"] + 4000, y = mx["y"], label = "maximum",
           hjust = 0, size = 3, colour = PAL$ink, family = "Helvetica") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = PAL$seq, name = "Likelihood ratio statistic",
                       labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) + scalebar_layer(bb) + north_layer(bb) +
  labs(title = "Where an agency would look first",
       subtitle = glue("Scan statistic surface, circles of {paste(attr(sc,'r')/1000, collapse=', ')} km.")) +
  theme_map()
```
