## Consistency across approaches

My first-order and second-order analyses agree where they should and disagree in two
places, and the disagreements taught me more than the agreement did.

**They agree on the dominant scale.** My inhomogeneous pair correlation function
peaks at `r round(EX$summary_ext$peak_r_m)` m. My Thomas process fitted to that same
curve returns a cluster standard deviation of `r fmt_n(sig_t)` m. Two estimates from
different machinery, one envelope-based and one model-based, both put the dominant
structure at roughly a kilometre. That agreement is the main reason I am willing to
quote a number.

**They disagree about extent, and it is the cumulative statistic that misled me.**
$L_{inhom}$ never re-enters its envelope within 20 km, which tempted me to conclude
that dependence extends at least that far. $g_{inhom}$, which localises scale
instead of accumulating it, shows the excess is within 10% of nothing by about
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. Both computations are
correct and the second is the one I report, because $L$ accumulates every excess at
smaller lags and therefore stays elevated long past the range over which anything is
actually happening. This is a general property of $K$ and $L$ rather than a quirk of
my data, and it is probably the single most useful thing I learned doing this
exercise.

**They disagree about sufficiency, and my first-order surface loses.** My earlier
version, capped at a 5 km lag, concluded that the intensity surface was an adequate
description above about 2 km. That was wrong, and wrong because of a decision rather
than a computation: my cap was too short to see where dependence ended. Corrected,
the first-order surface is not a sufficient description at any lag below roughly
`r round(EX$summary_ext$r_g_within_10pct_of_1/1000, 1)` km. A smooth intensity map is
still a reasonable tool for allocating resources across a regency. It is not a tool
for anticipating what happens next around a fire that has already started.

My covariate models sharpen this rather than softening it. They improve on an
intercept-only model by `r fmt_n(round(dn))` AIC units, so a lot of the first-order
variation is explained by accessibility. But the residual $K$ function shows they
capture none of the local interaction. Location explains where fire is likely. It
does not explain the contagion.

## Where my analysis is weakest

Four places, roughly in order of how much they worry me.

**My event definition does the heavy lifting.** Collapsing detections to cells is
defensible and I think necessary, but it is a modelling decision that I have
presented as data preparation, and I should be honest that those are not the same
thing. A cell that burned for three weeks and a cell that burned for one overpass
contribute identically to `ppp_cell`. If I weighted cells by persistence or by
cumulative radiative power I would be answering a related but different question,
and I am not certain I would reach the same conclusion about scale.

**My inhomogeneous null is estimated from the data I am testing.** The bias runs in
the conservative direction, so I am comfortable that the rejection stands. But the
*magnitude* of the excess clustering is not reliably estimated, so anything I say
about how much clustering there is should be read as ordinal rather than
quantitative.

**Detectability is confounded with intensity.** I cannot discharge assumptions A1
and A2 within this data source. Sub-surface peat smouldering, the mode I care most
about for public health, is systematically under-detected, and cloud cover is not
plausibly independent of location. What I have mapped is a surface of detected fire,
not of fire.

**One of my decisions was simply wrong and I had to reverse it.** I initially capped
the r range at 5 km. Every inhomogeneous statistic sat outside its envelope across
the whole of that range, which means my cap could not answer the question I set it
to answer, and my first draft drew a conclusion from it that the extended analysis
contradicts. I have left the cap in the record rather than quietly replacing it. A
range chosen before seeing the curves and then revised when the curves demanded it
is a different thing from a range chosen to produce a tidy answer, and a reader has
no way to tell those apart unless I say which one happened.

# Geovisualisation and geocommunication

Every figure carries its interpretation in its caption, inside the 150-word limit.
This section is about the rules I gave myself for the figures themselves, because
consistent encoding is what lets a reader compare one of my maps with another
instead of re-learning the graphic each time.

**One palette, used for one thing.** I use a single warm, perceptually ordered
sequential ramp for intensity in every map where intensity is the variable, and I
never use it for a categorical distinction. My one diverging scale encodes a
quantity that genuinely has a meaningful midpoint, the overall share of events in
the peak period, and I set the midpoint to that value rather than to the middle of
the data range. I kept the ramp warm even though the site's accent colour is teal,
because it is encoding fire and a teal heat map would fight its own subject.

**Square-root transformation, disclosed.** Fire intensity here spans roughly two
orders of magnitude, so a linear ramp renders the entire regency outside the peat
belt as one flat colour. I use a square-root scale so the structure of the lower
range stays visible. That decision changes what a reader sees, so I label it on
every scale that uses it rather than burying it.

**Statistical graphics and maps share a type system.** Same typeface, same rule
weights, same muted axis treatment across both, because my argument moves between
them continuously. I did not want a reader to experience the $L$ function and the
intensity map as coming from different documents.

**Scale and orientation on every map, at minimum weight.** A regency 213 km long
cannot be read without a scale bar. I drew the bar and north arrow as thin line work
rather than ornament, because they are reference furniture and should not compete
with the data.

**Uncertainty shown wherever it exists.** Envelope ribbons on every second-order
figure, confidence bands on the covariate curves, a normalisation note on the
space-time panels. A curve drawn without its envelope invites over-reading, and
over-reading is the exact failure this whole report is built to avoid.

**What I deliberately left out.** No three-dimensional surface: it would occlude
data and add nothing a colour ramp cannot carry. No basemap imagery: it would import
a visual texture I have not validated and imply a precision the 375 m grid does not
support. No interpolated surface beyond the window boundary, because my analysis has
no jurisdiction there.

# Public-safety planning and management

```{r}
#| label: ps-wordcount
#| include: false
# The brief caps this section at 500 words. Counted on render rather than trusted.
```

My findings support four operational conclusions, and I have tried to keep what the
evidence shows separate from what I am inferring.

**Direct evidence, usable now.** My intensity surface identifies where fire recurs
across a season at a resolution finer than any administrative unit. Roughly two
orders of magnitude separate the southern peat belt from the northern interior. So
resources allocated in proportion to sub-district area, or spread evenly, are badly
matched to risk. My surface supports a concrete reallocation: concentrate standing
capability in the southern third, and treat the northern interior as a response area
rather than a prevention area.

**Direct evidence, with a scale attached.** Two methods I ran independently agree
that the dominant clustering scale is about 1.1 km, with roughly 95% of a cluster's
events within 2.6 km of its centre. That gives a containment geometry I am willing
to defend: when a detection arrives, the area worth immediate attention is the
surrounding two to three kilometres, not the surrounding pixel and not the
surrounding sub-district. Measurable elevation runs out to about 7 km, so I would
treat 2.6 km as a first ring rather than a boundary. My Knox result adds the time
dimension: the raised probability of a neighbouring cell igniting is concentrated in
the first few days. A response window of days over a radius of kilometres is
supported by what I found.

**Direct evidence about monitoring, not about fire.** The day and night contrast is
an artefact of four fixed overpass times. Any dashboard reporting a daily fire cycle
from these data would be reporting the orbit, and I nearly made that mistake myself.
My pair correlation function also shows the analysis cannot resolve anything below
375 m, so these data cannot support tasking at the individual plot scale. That is a
limit on the instrument. Buying a finer answer needs a different sensor, not a
different statistic.

**Inference that needs information I do not have.** My association between intensity
and proximity to roads is strong, but roads get built where land is already worked,
so I cannot read it as a causal lever. Whether improving access aids suppression or
enables ignition is not answerable from what I have, and the two point in opposite
policy directions. Settling it needs ignition-cause records, land-tenure boundaries
and enforcement data.

My flat drainage relationship is also not evidence that drainage does not matter.
OpenStreetMap does not map the minor canal network of the former Mega Rice Project,
so my covariate is measuring mapping coverage. Testing that mechanism properly needs
a canal inventory and water-table observations.

Finally, the expansion from a southeastern origin describes one season, which is all
I have. Whether it recurs, and could therefore support early-season forecasting,
needs the multi-year record the ninety-day retention denied me. That is the next
thing I would do, and it is a data-access problem rather than a methodological one.

```{r tbl-repro}

tibble::tribble(
  ~Script, ~Purpose, ~Output,
  "`R/00_config.R`", "every study-design parameter, in one place", "sourced by all",
  "`R/01_acquire.R`", "download, retention probe, regency ranking", "`firms_raw.rds`, `kal_adm2.rds`, `regency_ranking.rds`, `retention_probe.rds`, `acquisition_log.md`",
  "`R/01b_fill_gaps.R`", "completeness audit, gap re-query with backoff, verification", "`gap_report.rds`",
  "`R/02_prepare.R`", "screening, audit trail, the three patterns", "`prepared.rds`, `qa_steps.rds`",
  "`R/03_firstorder.R`", "quadrats, bandwidths, KDE, FRP, temporal", "`firstorder.rds`",
  "`R/04_secondorder.R`", "G, F, L, pcf, inhomogeneous versions, global tests", "`secondorder.rds`",
  "`R/05_spacetime.R`", "Knox test, relative risk, trajectory, space-time KDE", "`spacetime.rds`",
  "`R/06_covariates_models.R`", "OSM covariates from the Geofabrik extract, ppm, AIC, residual K, scan test", "`covariates_models.rds`",
  "`R/07_cluster_scale.R`", "Thomas process by explicit minimum contrast, with and without the trend", "`thomas.rds`",
  "`R/08_extended_range.R`", "second-order statistics to a 20 km lag, plus a correction cross-check", "`extended.rds`",
  "`R/helpers.R`", "one theme and one palette for every figure", "sourced by report and slides"
) |> kable()
```

I fix the random seed at `r SEED` in `R/00_config.R` and set it at the top of every
analysis script, so all my Monte Carlo results reproduce exactly.

One engineering thing I hit that affects reproducibility in practice, and that I had
not expected. `spatstat`'s `fv` and `envelope` objects retain the closures used to
build them, and those closures capture the calling environment. Because my analysis
scripts hold several multi-megabyte caches in that environment, saving the objects
directly gave me an 843 MB file for `extended.rds` alone. I now convert each cache
to plain data frames before saving, which keeps every number and brings that same
file under a megabyte. The
geoBoundaries download is pinned to commit `9469f09` rather than to a moving
`current` endpoint. The FIRMS key is read from `.Renviron`, which is
git-ignored; `.Renviron.example` documents what is required.

```{r tbl-session}
#| label: tbl-session
#| tbl-cap: "The environment this report was rendered in."
si <- sessionInfo()
tibble::tibble(
  Component = c("R", "platform", "sf", "GDAL", "PROJ", "spatstat.explore",
                "spatstat.model", "ggplot2"),
  Version = c(paste(si$R.version$major, si$R.version$minor, sep = "."),
              si$platform, as.character(packageVersion("sf")),
              sf_extSoftVersion()[["GDAL"]], sf_extSoftVersion()[["PROJ"]],
              as.character(packageVersion("spatstat.explore")),
              as.character(packageVersion("spatstat.model")),
              as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")))) |> kable(align = "ll")
```
